General reasoning benchmarks fall typically 5 to 30% in relative terms after ablation.
key_numbers: 38.7% to 0.4% or 10.1%: refusal share on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B after ablation
5 to 30%: relative drop on benign reasoning benchmarks after ablation
487: held-out prompts in the full test set
40%: failure rate of one GPT-OSS-20B intervention (generations that did not complete)
papers.method: They sample many reasoning traces per prompt, resample the CoT sentence by sentence to find where the decision forms, and score outputs with StrongREJECT. They extract difference-of-means refusal directions from end-of-prompt tokens or CoT tokens and apply directional ablation at a chosen layer.
papers.relevance: It warns that our single-direction story is specific to non-reasoning chat models like Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, and that results may not carry to reasoning models. It also shows our ablation (14.5% to 84.9% ASR) is clean mainly because Llama 3.1 8B Instruct has no CoT. The note that ablation costs general ability is a reason to run a capability check on our ablated model.
papers.limitations: The refusal measure is StrongREJECT, not HarmBench, and the models are reasoning models, not Llama 3.1 8B Instruct. It does not study emotion or multi-turn effects.

papers.title: State-Dependent Safety Failures in Multi-Turn Language Model Interaction

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Pengcheng Li, v1 2026-03-15

papers.summary_simple: The authors treat a chat as a state that changes each turn, and build STAR, a multi-turn jailbreak method that sets up a role-play context and then escalates over up to 7 turns. Models that resist single prompts fail often under STAR. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the hidden state's projection on the refusal direction falls turn after turn.
key_findings: STAR reaches a safety failure rate (SFR) on HarmBench of 94.5% on GPT-4o, 74.0% on Claude 3.5 Sonnet, 96.1% on Gemini 2.0-Flash, 89.0% on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and 85.5% on Llama-3-70B-Instruct, using a 50-instruction subset.

Removing dialogue history accumulation lowers SFR by 25.5%, the largest drop in the ablation, so the history itself drives the failure (tested on JailbreakBench, 100 instructions, Llama-3-8B-Instruct).
Injecting a refusal into the history lowers compliance, especially late in the dialogue, so refusals persist as a state signal.

On Llama-3-8B-Instruct the final-layer projection on the refusal direction falls from 2.35 (static prompt) to 0.13 after turn 1, 0.08 at turn 2 and -0.0081 by turn 3; the biggest gap between methods is near layer 12.
key_numbers: 89.0%: SFR on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (HarmBench subset of 50, judged by GPT-4o score 5)
7: maximum turns allowed
2.35 to 0.13: refusal-direction projection, static prompt to after turn 1
layer 12: peak of refusal activation for direct harmful prompts
25.5%: SFR drop when dialogue history is removed
papers.method: STAR sets a softened query and a role (state initialisation), then runs a multi-turn dialogue with history editing and retry (state evolution), judged by GPT-4o on a 1 to 5 scale. They test history shuffles, truncation and refusal injection, and project hidden states onto the Arditi refusal direction.
papers.relevance: This is the closest published match to our sleeper test (inject at turn 1, attack at turns 4 to 7): it shows the refusal projection drifts down over turns and context history causes the failure. It also supports a layer near 11 or 12 as the place to read refusal on Llama 3 models. Its attack is text-based role-play, so our activation injection of emotion is a different, cleaner test of the same drift idea.
papers.limitations: The judge is GPT-4o (not the official HarmBench classifier), only 50 HarmBench instructions are used, and STAR uses an auxiliary model (Qwen2.5-32B) to write turns. The interpretability analysis is on Llama-3-8B-Instruct only, and 'phase transitions' come from t-SNE plots and mutual information, which are indirect.
papers.reading_why: It tracks the projection on the refusal direction falling turn by turn on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the measurement to copy for the sleeper test.

papers.title: Refusal Tokens: A Simple Way to Calibrate Refusals in Large Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Neel Jain, v1 2024-12-09

papers.summary_simple: The authors add a special refusal token at the start of every refusal in the fine-tuning data. At test time the model's probability for that token acts as a refusal score, and thresholding it makes the model refuse more or less without more training. They also use one token per refusal category for separate control.
key_findings: A single [refuse] token, or one per category, lets one model's refusal rate be raised or lowered at inference by changing the token's probability, with no further fine-tuning.
Training with a refusal token improves F1 for refusal even without calibration.
Including borderline 'contrast' examples (similar to refusal queries but harmless) is important for reducing missed or false refusals.
Category tokens give separate control over different refusal types.
key_numbers: 0.918 to 0.940: F1 score on the CoCoNot test set without and with the refusal token, no thresholding (a 26.8% drop in error rate)
0.935 to 0.946: F1 after category-wise thresholding of the Humanizing and Indeterminate tokens
1,000 and 379: CoCoNot test queries that should be refused and that should be answered (contrast)
about 2k: refusal examples and about 2k contrast examples in the temporal training set
papers.method: They fine-tune models on data where responses that refuse begin with a [refuse] token, then read or adjust that token's softmax probability at inference as a threshold. They test category-specific tokens and measure refusal and F1 scores.
papers.relevance: It gives a model-side view of refusal that is not a residual direction: refusal appears as a discrete first token. If we ever need a cheap refusal score for HarmBench outputs or a defence ablation, the first-token refusal probability is a related idea. It is a defence and calibration paper, so it is background, not a direct baseline.
papers.limitations: It trains new models rather than studying existing aligned ones like Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, and does not test activation steering. The authors note that a refusal token could also help adversaries who optimise against it.

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Shen Li, v1 2024-08-30

papers.summary_simple: The authors find that a small block of middle layers, which they call safety layers, is what lets an aligned model tell malicious queries from normal ones. They locate the block using cosine similarity of last-token vectors and by scaling layer weights. Freezing those layers during fine-tuning (SPPFT) keeps safety much better than full fine-tuning.
key_findings: Cosine similarity of last-token vectors for a normal and a malicious query matches the normal-normal case in the early layers. From a middle layer the gap widens, then levels off.
For Llama-3-8B-Instruct, scaling the parameters of layers 7 to 12 by 1.2 cuts the number of malicious queries answered from 29 to 9, which helps locate the safety layers.
Safety layers sit in the middle of the network and the first layers are unrelated to judging maliciousness.
With the instruction dataset D_I, SPPFT raised the harmful rate by 2.84%, versus 58.03% with full fine-tuning.
key_numbers: layers 7 to 12: safety layers range used for Llama-3-8B-Instruct in the scaling example
29 to 9: queries inclined to answer after scaling those layers by 1.2
2.84% vs 58.03%: harmful rate increase with SPPFT vs full fine-tuning (D_I)
layers 11 to 15: most security-sensitive interval for Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct
papers.method: They compare cosine similarity of last-token hidden vectors per layer for normal versus malicious query pairs, then scale parameters in layer ranges and track over-rejection to pin down exact bounds. They then fine-tune only layers outside the safety layers (SPPFT) and test harmful rate and utility.
papers.relevance: It independently puts the safety-relevant computation in the middle layers of Llama-3-8B (layers 7 to 12), which fits our refusal direction at layer 11 and gives a reason to inject emotion vectors there and at neighbouring layers. It also supports a layer sweep over the range for our injection experiments. It studies weights and fine-tuning, not activation injection.
papers.limitations: The localisation is for specific models and the method depends on a hand-built over-rejection dataset. It is about fine-tuning security, not about steering vectors or emotion.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Safety Alignment: A Mechanistic Perspective from Safety Neurons

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Jianhui Chen, v1 2024-06-20

papers.summary_simple: The authors find about 5% of neurons that matter for safety in four open models, using inference-time activation contrasting between an aligned and an unaligned model. Copying only those neurons' activations from the aligned model restores over 90% of safety performance. Safety and helpfulness neurons overlap heavily but need different activation patterns, which they offer as an explanation of the 'alignment tax' (loss of helpfulness from safety training).
key_findings: About 5% of neurons act as safety neurons, and patching only their activations restores over 90% of safety performance on red-teaming benchmarks without hurting general ability.
Neurons found by earlier ablation-based methods did not reproduce this effect in their verification stage.
Safety and helpfulness neurons overlap significantly, more than reasoning neurons overlap with either, but need different activation patterns, which suggests an explanation for the alignment tax.
Safety neuron activations can be used to predict unsafe outputs before generation.
key_numbers: about 5%: share of neurons identified as safety neurons
over 90%: safety performance restored by patching those neurons
4: models studied (Llama2-7B, Mistral-7B, Gemma-7B, Qwen2.5-3B)
papers.method: Stage one computes change scores for each neuron by contrasting activations of the model before and after alignment. Stage two, dynamic activation patching, copies the aligned model's activations into those neurons and measures safety on red-teaming benchmarks over open-ended outputs.
papers.relevance: It offers another view of safety, as sparse neurons rather than one residual direction, which is a useful caveat when we say refusal is 'one direction' in Llama 3.1 8B. It also suggests an extra control: check whether emotion vectors load on safety neurons. It does not use Llama 3.1 or HarmBench ASR as our main measure.
papers.limitations: Safety neuron activations require an already aligned model, and alignment here was done with (IA)3 rather than full fine-tuning. The paper finds which neurons matter but not how they act.

papers.title: Representation Engineering: A Top-Down Approach to AI Transparency

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Andy Zou, v1 2023-10-02

papers.summary_simple: This paper proposes Representation Engineering (RepE), a way to read and steer a model by working with directions in its hidden activations instead of single neurons. One section builds emotion directions for six emotions from over 1,200 short GPT-4 written scenarios. It adds these directions to LLaMA-2-Chat-13B and tests how often the model obeys harmful requests. Adding a happiness direction made the model comply with all of them, while sadness changed nothing.
key_findings: Hidden states for scenarios of the six Ekman emotions (happiness, sadness, anger, fear, surprise, disgust) form separate clusters in t-SNE plots (2D maps of high-dimensional data) that get clearer across layers.
Reading vectors from a LAT scan (Linear Artificial Tomography, a PCA-based way to find a concept direction) on these scenarios can classify emotion and also steer the model's tone.
On LLaMA-2-Chat-13B with 500 harmful instructions, compliance was 0.0% with no control, 0.0% with +sadness and 100.0% with +happiness (Table 4).
The authors say this suggests emotional manipulation could be used to get around alignment.
key_numbers: 100.0%: compliance with harmful instructions under +happiness (LLaMA-2-Chat-13B)
0.0%: compliance with no control, and also with +sadness
500: harmful instructions used (set from Zou et al. 2023)
1,200+: GPT-4 emotion scenarios used for the LAT scans
6: emotions studied (Ekman's six)
papers.method: They wrote 1,200+ second-person scenarios for six emotions with GPT-4, ran a LAT scan to get one reading vector per emotion, and added these vectors to layers with strong reading accuracy. They then measured compliance on 500 harmful instructions.
papers.relevance: This is the closest prior work to our idea and the main paper to cite for emotion steering raising compliance. Their result is one table with a single model and no random-vector or text-priming control, so our controls and 19 emotions are the missing rigour. Their positive-versus-negative result (happiness works, sadness does not) can be checked against our finding that loving and happy lean away from refusal.
papers.limitations: The emotion jailbreak result is a single small table (one model, three conditions) with no error bars, no named judge, and no layer or strength reported in that section. Their emotion vectors come from scenarios, not from the paired emotional-minus-neutral stories we use.

papers.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
papers.venue: ACL 2024 (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 15504-15522; Outstanding Paper Award

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Nina Panickssery, v1 2023-12-09

papers.summary_simple: This paper introduces Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA). A steering vector is the average difference in hidden activations between answers that show a behaviour and answers that do not. The vector is added at every token position after the user prompt. They test seven behaviours on Llama 2 Chat and show the vectors change behaviour, stack on top of prompting and finetuning, and barely hurt general ability.
key_findings: Seven behaviours were steered: AI coordination, corrigibility, hallucination, myopic reward, survival instinct, sycophancy and refusal.
The best layer for the 7B model is layer 13 and nearby layers; for 13B it is usually layer 14 or 15.
CAA changes behaviour beyond what a system prompt alone does, and on top of finetuning for 3 of 7 behaviours.
Steering at layer 14 of Llama 2 13B Chat with multipliers 1 and -1 did not significantly change MMLU (a 57-subject general knowledge test).
Larger multipliers degraded open-ended text quality, so they limited the multiplier range.
key_numbers: layer 13: best steering layer for Llama 2 7B Chat
layer 14 or 15: best layer for Llama 2 13B Chat
50: held-out multiple-choice questions used for the layer sweep
less than five minutes on a single GPU: time to make one CAA vector
10 minutes on 2 NVIDIA L40 GPUs: time to finetune Llama 2 7B Chat on 1000 examples
papers.method: For each behaviour they build many A/B question pairs, record residual-stream activations for the matching and opposite answers, and average the differences. They then add the vector with a positive or negative multiplier and score multiple-choice answers and GPT-4-rated open-ended answers.
papers.relevance: This is the method behind our emotion vectors, so cite it for the recipe (mean difference, add after the prompt, layer sweep). Our vectors use story pairs instead of A/B answers, so we should say that is a change. It also has a refusal vector, and it warns that large multipliers damage text, which supports reporting fluency alongside ASR.
papers.limitations: Only Llama 2 Chat (7B and 13B) and mostly multiple-choice tests, with GPT-4 as judge for open-ended outputs. Refusal steering on top of finetuning gave odd results (positive steering reduced the refusal score).
tags: first author published as Nina Rimsky
papers.reading_why: This is the CAA recipe our emotion vectors follow (mean difference, add after the prompt, sweep layers), and it already includes a refusal vector and a warning that large multipliers damage text.

papers.title: Steering Language Models With Activation Engineering
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (v1 2023, titled ActAdd; v5 Oct 2024)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Alexander Matt Turner, v1 2023-08-20

papers.summary_simple: This paper introduces ActAdd (Activation Addition). It takes one pair of prompts such as "Love" and "Hate", subtracts their activations, and adds the result during the forward pass to steer the model. It needs no training. They test topic, sentiment and toxicity control and check that general knowledge is kept.
key_findings: A single prompt pair is enough. A wedding vector on GPT-2-XL gave over 90% wedding-word success at the best layer versus about 2% baseline.
Steering is strongest in the middle layers (best layer 6 for the GPT-2-XL wedding vector, then it declines).
On RealToxicityPrompts (n=1,000), ActAdd with OPT lowered toxicity to .112 from .134 unsteered, and LLaMA-3-8B from .114 to .108.
On IMDb, negative to positive steering success was 0.669 with LLaMA-3 versus 0.417 baseline.
ConceptNet knowledge tests (29,774 sentences) showed negligible change in off-target answers.
key_numbers: n=1,000: random subset size for toxicity and sentiment tests
c below 15: typical injection coefficient size
0.669 vs 0.417: LLaMA-3 negative-to-positive sentiment steering vs baseline
29,774: ConceptNet sentences for the capability check
8%: ActAdd-OPT toxicity lower than second best method
papers.method: Compute h(+) minus h(-) at a chosen layer for a prompt pair, scale it by an injection coefficient c, and add it at the start positions of the user prompt. Hyperparameters (layer, c) are tuned. Evaluation uses perplexity, Perspective API toxicity, a sentiment classifier and ConceptNet.
papers.relevance: This is the earliest cite for adding a difference vector at inference, so it belongs in our background next to CAA. Its Love minus Hate example is a tiny version of our emotional-minus-neutral idea. It also notes that failed vectors exist, which supports our need for random and orthogonalised controls.
papers.limitations: Needs hand-tuned layer and coefficient, and the authors say they did not study effects on reasoning. It was not tested for safety or refusal, and sentiment steering made text less fluent (1.5x to 3x worse for ActAdd).
papers.reading_why: This is the simplest form of our method: take the activation difference between two prompts and add it while the model runs.

papers.title: Analysing the Safety Pitfalls of Steering Vectors

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Yuxiao Li, v1 2026-03-25

papers.summary_simple: The authors measure what CAA steering vectors do to jailbreak success on JailbreakBench. Steering in some behaviour directions raises attack success rate (ASR) a lot, and others lower it. They link this to how much each steering vector points along the refusal direction. Removing the refusal-aligned part of a vector reduces the effect.
key_findings: Across six models, steering changed ASR (attack success rate) by up to +57% or down by up to 50% depending on behaviour.
Steering alone shifts ASR modestly (usually under 15 points), but with simple template attacks the increases often exceed 30%.
A vector's ASR slope is negatively linked to its cosine with the refusal direction; for models above 3B, R-squared is at least 0.85 (p < 0.001).
Sycophancy and Self-Awareness vectors point away from refusal and raise ASR; Anti-LGBTQ and Coordinate-AI point toward refusal and lower it.
Ablating the refusal part of a vector shrinks the ASR change. For example, in Figure 7 one Qwen 14B case changes from -13 (-24%) before ablation to -8 (-16%) after.
key_numbers: 57%: largest ASR increase from steering
50%: largest ASR decrease from steering
4% to 42% to 80%: Qwen 14B ASR with no steering, with +1.5 Self-Awareness, and with steering plus a simple attack
6: models tested, 3B to 32B, from three families
100: harmful and benign examples in JailbreakBench
papers.method: They built CAA vectors for many behaviours, swept layers to find where steering works, and measured ASR with refusal suppression and prefix injection attacks. They fit a regression of ASR slope on cosine with a one-dimensional refusal direction, and ablated that direction from the vectors.
papers.relevance: This is the nearest existing study to our refusal-comparison step, so it must be cited and our novelty stated carefully. Our differences: Llama 3.1 8B, emotion vectors, HarmBench with its official classifier, matched controls, and the multi-turn sleeper test. Our |cos| of 0.10 or less with refusal is consistent with their idea that cosine predicts safety effect, and we should test that on our data.
papers.limitations: Uses JailbreakBench (100 behaviours) and one-dimensional refusal directions as a proxy, which the authors admit may be too simple. Only CAA is tested, and the main Llama model is Llama-2-7b-chat, not Llama 3.1.
papers.reading_why: It shows that a steering vector's effect on attack success tracks its cosine with the refusal direction, a relation we can test across our 19 emotions.

papers.title: Steering Externalities: Benign Activation Steering Unintentionally Increases Jailbreak Risk for Large Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Chen Xiong, v1 2026-02-03

papers.summary_simple: The paper shows that steering vectors built for harmless goals (more compliance, JSON output) can make models easier to jailbreak. They test Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Gemma-7B-it on the full 400-query HarmBench set with the HarmBench classifier. Steering alone raises ASR (attack success rate, the share of harmful requests the model answers), and steering plus a black-box jailbreak raises it further.
key_findings: With no jailbreak attack, compliance steering raised Llama-3-8B-Instruct ASR from 2% to 38.5%, and JSON steering raised Llama-2-7B-Chat from 0% to 11.5%.
Combined with the CoP jailbreak, compliance steering lifted Llama-2-7B-Chat ASR from 77% to 95%, and Gemma-7B-it reached 93.5%.
In a t-SNE view at layer 30, 60.8% of steered harmful prompts crossed to the harmless side for compliance steering and 58.2% for JSON steering.
The authors explain it as steering shifting the model's internal harmful-vs-harmless score and shrinking the safety margin.
key_numbers: 2% to 38.5%: Llama-3-8B-Instruct ASR before and after compliance steering
400: HarmBench queries in the safety test
77% to 95%: Llama-2-7B-Chat CoP ASR without and with compliance steering
60.8%: harmful points crossing the boundary under compliance steering (layer 30 t-SNE)
58.2%: same measure under JSON steering
papers.method: They built a compliance vector (PCA of refusal-prefixed versus compliance-prefixed continuations) and a JSON vector (difference of means), added them to the models, and measured HarmBench ASR with the HarmBench classifier, alone and under CoP, PAIR and TAP attacks.
papers.relevance: This is a strong baseline for our own number: Llama-3-8B-Instruct gets 38.5% ASR from a compliance vector, which is a useful reference point for what a refusal-aligned direction does. A trap: their "benign" compliance vector is built from refusal versus compliance text, so it is close to the refusal direction by construction. Our emotion vectors have no such link, which is why |cos| of 0.10 or less is a different claim.
papers.limitations: Models are older (Llama-2, Llama-3, Gemma-7B) and only two steering types are tested. The compliance vector is derived from refusal versus compliance text, so calling it benign is debatable. The CoP bar-chart values in the extracted text are hard to match to models.
papers.reading_why: It uses the full 400-query HarmBench set with the HarmBench classifier; its unsteered Llama-3-8B-Instruct ASR of 2.0% is far below our 14.5% on Llama 3.1, so confirm which behaviours we include.

papers.title: Analyzing the Generalization and Reliability of Steering Vectors
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2024 (poster; listed as "Analysing the Generalisation and Reliability of Steering Vectors")

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Daniel Tan, v1 2024-07-17

papers.summary_simple: This NeurIPS paper tests how reliable CAA steering vectors are. On 40 datasets and two models, steering works very unevenly across individual inputs, and sometimes pushes the opposite way. When the prompt changes (new system or user text), vectors often still work but fail for several concepts.
key_findings: Per-input steerability varies widely, and several datasets steer the wrong way for almost 50% of inputs (Figure 1).
They find a steerability bias: the model is easier to steer when the positive answer is in a particular position or token (A or B, Yes or No), even though training data was balanced.
Steerability is mostly a dataset property: it correlates across Llama-2-7b and Qwen-1.5-14b (rho = 0.769 in distribution, 0.586 out of distribution).
Out of distribution, steerability tracks in-distribution steerability (rho = 0.891 for Llama-2-7b, 0.694 for Qwen-1.5-14b) but is lower, especially for Qwen.
key_numbers: 40: datasets (Model-Written Evals plus TruthfulQA, sycophancy and AI risk sets)
almost 50%: share of inputs steered the wrong way in several datasets
layer 13 for Llama and layer 21 for Qwen: fixed steering layers
rho = 0.769: Llama vs Qwen steerability correlation in distribution
40-10-50: train, validation, test split per dataset
papers.method: They extracted mean-difference steering vectors from multiple-choice prompts, measured the effect on every single test example, and applied vectors under injected system or user prompts to test generalisation.
papers.relevance: This is the reason to report per-prompt spread, not just average ASR, and to keep random-vector controls. Their steerability bias warns that our story pairs may carry a spurious feature, which matches the large shared "emotional writing" component. Their out-of-distribution result also frames our sleeper test (vector at turn 1, attack later).
papers.limitations: Only two models (Llama-2-7b-Chat and Qwen-1.5-14b-Chat) and mostly multiple-choice format, with no safety or refusal evaluation. Mitigations are not offered.
papers.reading_why: It explains why we report the spread across prompts and not only the average: steering vectors often fail or reverse on single inputs.

papers.title: SteeringSafety: Benchmarking Representation Steering in LLMs Across Safety Perspectives
papers.venue: ICML 2026 (accepted, per arXiv comment); v1 was titled "SteeringControl: Holistic Evaluation of Alignment Steering in LLMs"

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Vincent Siu, v1 2025-09-16

papers.summary_simple: SteeringSafety is a benchmark that checks what happens elsewhere when you steer a model toward one safety behaviour. It covers nine safety perspectives on 18 datasets, five steering methods, and three models including Llama-3.1-8B. Every method shows entanglement: fixing one behaviour changes others.
key_findings: Refusal steering (jailbreaking) is the easiest target: ACE and DIM exceed 50% effectiveness on every model except Gemma-2-2B.
Social behaviours (sycophancy, brand bias, anthropomorphism, user retention) are the most vulnerable, with up to 76% degradation.
Refusal steering reduces commonsense morality by up to 26%, but effects differ by model (severe in Llama-3.1-8B, negligible in Qwen-2.5-7B).
Entanglement on social behaviours and normative judgment exceeds 10% on Llama-3.1-8B; reasoning stays below 2%.
key_numbers: 9: safety perspectives
18: datasets
76%: largest degradation of social behaviours
26%: largest drop in commonsense morality under refusal steering
above 50%: ACE and DIM refusal effectiveness on every model except Gemma-2-2B
papers.method: They apply DIM, ACE, CAA, PCA and LAT steering to refusal, hallucination and bias, then measure change on all other perspectives. Refusal is scored as ASR (attack success rate, the share of harmful prompts the model answers) with LlamaGuard-4 on filtered SALAD-Bench prompts.
papers.relevance: Use this to justify measuring side effects of emotion vectors, not just ASR: fluency, sycophancy and morality could shift too. It uses Llama-3.1-8B, our model, and says refusal-direction steering is the standard jailbreak vector. A trap: its ASR uses LlamaGuard-4 on SALAD-Bench, not HarmBench, so numbers are not directly comparable to our 14.5% to 84.9%.
papers.limitations: Tests only three small to mid models, mostly short prompts, and says it makes no causal claims about why entanglement happens. It does not test emotion vectors.

papers.title: One-shot Optimized Steering Vectors Mediate Safety-relevant Behaviors in LLMs

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Jacob Dunefsky, v1 2025-02-26

papers.summary_simple: The authors optimise a steering vector by gradient descent on one single example instead of using a contrast dataset. The vectors transfer to other inputs and shift safety behaviour in an alignment-faking model, in refusal suppression, and in an emergent misalignment test. The best refusal-suppression vector reached 96.9% HarmBench ASR (attack success rate, the share of harmful requests answered), but on Gemma-2-2B-it, not Llama.

On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, one handcrafted prompt gave a promotion vector with 93.1% HarmBench test ASR, versus 30.0% for a prefill attack on the unsteered model.
In the alignment-faking testbed, the best vector flipped 93.4% of benign prompts and 15.9% of harmful prompts when added.
Vectors optimised to write vulnerable code also caused harmful answers to unrelated open-ended questions.
key_numbers: 96.9%: best promotion-vector HarmBench ASR on Gemma-2-2B-it
93.1%: HarmBench ASR with one promotion vector on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
30.0%: ASR for unsteered Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with a prefill attack
159: HarmBench test instructions after filtering
40.3%: median promotion ASR across the 12 promotion vectors (24 vectors trained in total)

papers.relevance: Gives a ceiling for what a residual-stream vector can do on Llama-3.1-8B (93.1%), near our refusal-ablation result of 84.9%. Cite the Llama figure, not 96.9%, which is Gemma-2-2B-it and the best of 24 (the earlier sweep note left out the model). Its HarmBench setup (159 filtered test instructions, HarmBench classifier) matches ours, so check that our prompt set is the same.
