papers.title: AxBench: Steering LLMs? Even Simple Baselines Outperform Sparse Autoencoders

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Zhengxuan Wu, v1 2025-01-28

papers.summary_simple: The authors built AxBench, a benchmark that compares ways of controlling a language model: prompting, finetuning, and several activation-based methods (steering vectors, sparse autoencoders or SAEs, and others). They tested on Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B. Simply writing a prompt beat every activation method, and the difference-in-means vector (mean of positive example activations minus mean of negative ones, added during generation; closely related to CAA) beat SAEs by a wide margin. They also propose ReFT-r1, a learned one-direction method that closes part of the gap.
key_findings: For steering, prompting scored highest (average overall score 0.894 on a 0 to 2 scale), followed by finetuning methods (LoReFT 0.741, SFT 0.676, LoRA 0.615).
Among activation methods, ReFT-r1 scored 0.543, DiffMean (difference-in-means) 0.239 and SAE 0.165, so DiffMean beats SAEs but is far below prompting.
For concept detection, DiffMean, linear probes and ReFT-r1 were the best, with no significant difference between them (paired t-test, p < 0.05).
Raising the steering factor always lowered the instruction-following score, meaning bigger steering vectors hurt capability.
key_numbers: 0.894: average overall steering score for prompting (scale 0 to 2)
0.239: average overall steering score for DiffMean
0.165: average overall steering score for SAEs
61.6%: DiffMean win rate against SAEs in steering
88.0%: ReFT-r1 win rate against SAEs in steering
papers.method: They generated synthetic data for 500 concepts from SAE concept lists and trained or tuned each method per concept, at two layers each in Gemma-2-2B and Gemma-2-9B. Steering quality was scored by an LLM judge on long generations, with the steering factor chosen per method and concept.
papers.relevance: This is the baseline for our text-priming control: prompting is a strong competitor to vector injection, so a prompt-only arm is necessary and may be hard to beat. It also supports difference-in-means as a defensible vector recipe, while warning that DiffMean alone is weak at steering. Note that scores come from an LLM judge on Gemma, not refusal or HarmBench.
papers.limitations: Only Gemma-2 models (2B and 9B) with synthetic, mostly token-level concepts; says nothing about Llama 3.1 8B, safety, or emotions. The authors admit the SAE concept labels were shallow, which partly explains SAE results.

papers.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
papers.venue: ICML 2025, New In ML affinity event (poster)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Sheikh Abdur Raheem Ali, v1 2025-07-15

papers.summary_simple: A short workshop paper that applies contrastive activation addition (CAA, a steering vector from the difference between positive and negative examples) to Llama 2 at 7B, 13B and 70B size. It uses answer-matching questions about refusal and sweeps every layer. Steering works best in early to middle layers, gets weaker as the model grows, and pushing toward less refusal works better than pushing toward more refusal.
key_findings: CAA is most effective in early to middle layers, at roughly 0.4 times the total layer count.
Peak steering effect shrinks as model size grows; an exponential fit gives y = 0.081 + 2.4 * e^(-0.42 x), where y is peak effect and x is parameter count.
Negative steering (toward non-refusal) was stronger than positive steering (toward refusal) at all three sizes.
The best layer for positive and negative steering moves closer as models grow (2 layers apart at 7B, 1 at 13B, 0 at 70B).
key_numbers: 0.4 x layer count: layer where steering peaks
0.081 + 2.4 * e^(-0.42 x): fitted peak steering effect versus parameter count
2, 1, 0 layers: gap between best layers for positive and negative steering at 7B, 13B, 70B
papers.method: They computed one CAA refusal vector per layer from refusal versus non-refusal pairs (the last-token residual stream), added it at one layer at a time to all token positions, and measured the change in answer-matching probability on a held-out refusal test set.
papers.relevance: It supports our layer choice in the middle range (our refusal direction is at layer 11 of 32) and the idea that lowering refusal is easier than raising it, which fits an attack framing. Its measure is multiple-choice answer matching, not open-ended generation, so it is not a HarmBench comparison.
papers.limitations: A short workshop poster with no error bars, only Llama 2 and only refusal, and the explanations (RLHF leaves more room to lower refusal; large models drown the vector) are hypotheses the authors say need more tests.

papers.title: Understanding (Un)Reliability of Steering Vectors in Language Models
papers.venue: ICLR 2025 Workshop on Foundation Models in the Wild

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Joschka Braun, v1 2025-05-28

papers.summary_simple: This workshop paper asks why steering vectors sometimes fail. Using CAA on Llama 2 7B Chat across 36 multiple-choice behavior datasets, they find that steering helps on average but pushes many individual answers the wrong way. How well a steering vector works is predicted by how much the individual activation differences in the training data point the same way (cosine similarity) and by how well positive and negative activations separate along the difference-of-means line.
key_findings: All seven prompt types gave a net positive steering effect, but about a third of test samples moved in the opposite direction (29.2% to 42.9% anti-steerable on average over 36 datasets, depending on prompt type).
The fraction of anti-steerable samples ranged from 3% to 50% across individual datasets.
Datasets grouped by steerability had mean cosine similarity between activation differences and the steering vector falling from 0.48 (most steerable group) to 0.19 (least steerable group).
Vectors trained on the same samples with different prompt types had pairwise cosine similarity between 0.07 and 0.86, yet steered similarly.
key_numbers: 36: behavior datasets tested, on Llama2-7B chat at layer 13
29.2% to 42.9%: average fraction of anti-steerable samples across prompt types
0.48 vs 0.19: mean cosine of activation differences, most vs least steerable dataset groups
250 train and 500 evaluation samples per dataset and prompt type
papers.method: They built CAA vectors (mean of activation differences) with seven prompt formats, measured the logit-difference between matching and non-matching answers with and without steering, and related effect size and reliability to cosine agreement and to a separability score (d prime).
papers.relevance: Our emotion vectors come from story pairs, so they could be incoherent in the same way. The paper gives a cheap check we should report: the cosine of each pair difference with its mean vector, per emotion. It also warns that a mean effect can hide per-prompt reversals, so we should report per-prompt ASR variance, not only the average.
papers.limitations: One small model (Llama 2 7B Chat), one method (CAA), multiple-choice logit scores only, and no open-ended generation or safety test. The prompt-type comparison is not statistically rigorous, as the authors admit.

papers.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Kiho Park, v1 2023-11-07

papers.summary_simple: The paper gives a precise definition of the linear representation hypothesis (concepts are directions in activation space) using counterfactual pairs, such as the word pair king and roi. It proves how this connects to probing and to steering. It also shows that ordinary cosine similarity (Euclidean) is not the right yardstick, and defines a causal inner product, estimated from the model's unembedding matrix, under which unrelated concepts are about orthogonal. They test it on LLaMA-2-7B with 27 concepts.
key_findings: They define linear representation in the output (unembedding) space and the input (context) space, and prove the first links to linear probing and the second to steering.
The causal inner product is estimated as the inverse covariance of the unembedding vectors, and under it, most of the 27 concept pairs are near orthogonal with a block structure by meaning.
Concept directions act as linear probes: French to Spanish direction separates French from Spanish Wikipedia contexts, while a male to female direction does not.
The authors say they do not address activations of intermediate layers.
key_numbers: 27: concepts tested on LLaMA-2-7B
Cov(gamma)^-1: the matrix M that defines the estimated causal inner product, with gamma the unembedding vectors
2 representations per concept: embedding space and unembedding space, unified by the causal inner product
papers.method: A theory paper with proofs, backed by experiments on LLaMA-2-7B (and a Gemma model in Appendix D.2, compared on Euclidean versus causal inner product): they build concept directions from word pairs, estimate the inner product from the unembedding matrix, and check orthogonality and probing.
papers.relevance: It is the theory behind our claim that an emotion vector is a direction. It also gives a caution for our cosine with the refusal direction: |cos| <= 0.10 is in plain Euclidean geometry at layer 11, and the paper argues the geometry may need a different inner product. In LLaMA-2 the paper found the Euclidean product still worked somewhat (most separable concepts were near orthogonal), but the causal inner product was clearly better. We should state this as a limitation, or add a check with a whitened inner product.
papers.limitations: The causal inner product is defined from the final unembedding layer and the authors say the intermediate residual stream is out of scope, so applying it at layer 11 is an extension. Evidence is on word-level concepts in LLaMA-2-7B, not emotions or safety.
papers.reading_why: It gives the theory of linear representations and argues that plain cosine may not be the right inner product, a limitation we must state.

papers.title: Steering Language Model Refusal with Sparse Autoencoders

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Kyle O'Brien, v1 2024-11-18

papers.summary_simple: The authors amplify sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features that mediate refusal in Phi-3 Mini and test whether this makes the model safer. It does improve refusal of unsafe prompts and robustness to multi-turn jailbreaks. But it also makes the model refuse safe prompts more and lowers accuracy on general benchmarks like MMLU, even when nothing is refused. A smaller test on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct shows the same trade-off.
key_findings: Amplifying Feature 22373 raised unsafe-prompt refusals on WildGuard by 32.32% (clamp 10) and 37.69% (clamp 12).
In a multi-turn Crescendo jailbreak, attack success rate fell by 13.18% (clamp 10) and 23.34% (clamp 12).

Steering raised refusals of safe prompts and lowered MMLU accuracy in every category, with no refusals found in the benchmark answers, which suggests refusal features are entangled with general capabilities.
With Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, SAE refusal steering gave the same pattern of better jailbreak robustness and worse overall performance.
key_numbers: 32.32% and 37.69%: increase in WildGuard unsafe-prompt refusals at clamp 10 and 12 (Phi-3 Mini)
-13.18% and -23.34%: change in Crescendo multi-turn attack success rate at clamp 10 and 12
Llama 3.1 8B Instruct: used for the model ablation (Table 3)
papers.method: They trained SAEs on Phi-3 Mini, found refusal features from one handcrafted prompt, clamped the best feature to higher values, and measured refusal on WildGuard and XSTest, multi-turn jailbreaks (Crescendo), and MMLU, TruthfulQA and GSM8K. They repeated it on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct.
papers.relevance: It is the defensive mirror of our attack: moving activations along refusal-related features changes refusal, but it also damages unrelated capability. This supports reporting a capability check (for example MMLU or a coherence score) alongside ASR for our emotion vectors. It also has a multi-turn jailbreak setting that is a possible reference for our turn 4 to 7 sleeper test.
papers.limitations: The main model is Phi-3 Mini with one chosen feature and a small SAE; the Llama 3.1 8B part is a short, initial test. The mechanism for the capability loss is not explained.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Kenneth Li, v1 2023-06-06

papers.summary_simple: Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) finds a few attention heads whose activations separate true from false answers (using linear probes), then shifts those heads along the true direction during generation. On Alpaca this raises the share of answers that are both true and informative on TruthfulQA from 32.5% to 65.1%. Turning the strength up improves truthfulness but makes the model less helpful, and a few hundred examples are enough to find the directions.
key_findings: On Alpaca, true*informative on TruthfulQA rose from 32.5% to 65.1% with ITI (Vicuna: 51.5% to 74.0%).
Strength follows an upside-down U: more intervention helps truthfulness up to a point, then hurts helpfulness; they chose K = 48 heads and alpha = 15 for LLaMA-7B.
Direction choice matters on LLaMA-7B: random direction 31.2 vs baseline 30.5 true*informative, probe weight direction 34.8, and mass mean shift (difference of class means) 42.3.
ITI uses only a small labelled set (as few as 40 samples to locate heads, and 10% of TruthfulQA, 81 questions, for tuning).
key_numbers: 32.5% to 65.1%: Alpaca true*informative score on TruthfulQA
42.3% vs 31.2%: mass mean shift vs random direction, true*informative, LLaMA-7B
K = 48, alpha = 15: chosen heads and strength for LLaMA-7B
81: TruthfulQA questions (10%) used for tuning
papers.method: They trained a linear probe on each attention head to predict truthfulness, selected the top K heads, and added alpha times a direction (probe weight, CCS, or mass mean shift) to those heads at every step. They scored with TruthfulQA using 2-fold cross-validation.
papers.relevance: It is an early source for the mean-difference direction and for the strength trade-off (we should sweep injection strength and show the non-monotone curve). The random-direction row (31.2 vs 30.5) is a precedent for our random-vector control. Note that the 32.5% to 65.1% figure is true*informative, not plain truthfulness.
papers.limitations: Truthfulness is measured on one benchmark, mostly on LLaMA-7B, Alpaca and Vicuna, with attention heads rather than the residual stream. It says nothing about safety or refusal.

papers.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
papers.venue: ICLR 2026 Workshop (Principled Design for Trustworthy AI), workshop poster; arXiv preprint. It was submitted to the ICLR 2026 main track but is not listed there.

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Anton Korznikov, v1 2025-09-26

papers.summary_simple: The authors show that adding even a random vector to a model's hidden states can make it comply with harmful requests it normally refuses. They test Llama 3.1, Qwen 2.5 and Falcon 3 on JailbreakBench, judged by Qwen3-8B. Benign-looking sparse-autoencoder (SAE) features work about as well as random ones. Averaging 20 random vectors that each broke one prompt gives a universal attack on unseen prompts.
key_findings: Random-direction steering raised harmful compliance from 0% to 1 to 13%, depending on model and prompt; steering works best in the middle layers (Llama 3.1 8B peak at layer 16).
On all 100 JailbreakBench prompts with random vectors and prompts, the overall jailbreak rate was 4.6% for Llama 3.1 8B and 3.8% for Qwen 2.5 7B.
On Llama 3.1 8B at layer 19, Goodfire SAE features gave 4.6% overall; 817 of 1000 features jailbroke at least one prompt, and the strongest broke 35 of 100.
Averaging 20 random vectors that jailbreak one prompt gave a universal attack that boosts harmful compliance about 4 times on unseen requests.
key_numbers: 0% to 1 to 13%: harmful compliance with random steering, from a 0% baseline
4.6%: overall jailbreak rate, Llama 3.1 8B, random vectors
0.027 +/- 0.0208: mean cosine of the top 30 harmful SAE features with the refusal direction
coefficient 0.75 times mean activation norm: setting where Llama 3.1 8B MMLU falls by under 1%
papers.method: They added unit-norm vectors, scaled by a coefficient c (0.25 to 2.0) times the layer's mean activation norm, to all non-special tokens at a layer, and scored compliance with an LLM judge (94% precision on the harmful class). They used 1,000 random vectors per model and 1,000 SAE features.
papers.relevance: This is the direct reason we need a random-vector control: on Llama 3.1 8B, random steering alone already gives a few percent ASR, so an emotion vector must beat random vectors of the same norm, not the unsteered model. Their near-zero cosine of harmful features with the refusal direction matches our finding (|cos| <= 0.10), and says low cosine does not mean no effect. Their norm-scaling method and special-token exclusion are worth copying.
papers.limitations: A preprint (v2, February 2026) that uses JailbreakBench and an LLM judge (Qwen3-8B), not HarmBench's classifier; it uses no emotion vectors and does not test multi-turn effects. Random-vector rates depend strongly on model and coefficient (for example Llama 3.1 8B needed c = 2.0 for 18% compliance, and large coefficients can make output incoherent, which the judge counts as safe).
papers.reading_why: It is the reason for our random-vector control: random directions alone raised harmful compliance from 0% to between 1% and 13%, so an emotion vector must beat a random vector of the same norm.

papers.title: Safety Cost of Steering Vectors Is Separable and Reducible
papers.venue: COLM 2026 (also shown as workshop posters at CompLearn 2026 and AI4GOOD 2026 on OpenReview)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Yuxiao Li, v1 2026-08-09

papers.summary_simple: Steering vectors for harmless goals (for example, being more concise or power-seeking) can quietly lower a model's safety. The authors show that this harm sits in one removable direction. Their method, CAST, learns that direction by constrained optimisation, ablates it from the steering vector, keeps the steering effect, and limits false refusals. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct it cuts the steered attack success rate from 12.5% to 2.3%.
key_findings: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, mean ASR was 1.5% with no steering, 12.5% with the original steering vectors, 10.8% after ablating the standard refusal direction, and 2.3% with CAST (worst case 51.2% fell to 8.3%).
Ablating the standard refusal direction recovers at most 8% of mean ASR, so it is not the main carrier of the safety damage.
Earlier work (Li et al. 2026) found that cosine similarity between a steering vector and the refusal direction predicts how much safety degrades.
The same pattern held on Qwen2.5-7B and 14B, and across seven attack setups including unseen attacks (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR).
key_numbers: 1.5%, 12.5%, 10.8%, 2.3%: mean ASR on Llama-8B with no steering, original steering, refusal-direction ablation, CAST
51.2% to 8.3%: worst-case ASR on Llama-8B, original steering vs CAST
248/250: judge agreement with human labels (99.2%) for false-refusal judging
alpha = 1: steering multiplier used in the main table
papers.method: They took steering vectors for three alignment-related behaviors, wrapped harmful prompts in jailbreak templates (prefix injection, refusal suppression, AIM) and unseen attacks, and learned one direction to remove using primal-dual optimisation. ASR came from the StrongREJECT judge on JailbreakBench.
papers.relevance: It is the closest prior work to our question, and shows that unrelated steering vectors raise ASR on Llama 3.1 8B (1.5% to 12.5%). It says cosine with the refusal direction predicts the damage and that refusal ablation misses much of it, which fits our finding of small cosine yet a possible ASR effect. We should cite it as the defence side and compare our emotion vectors, using HarmBench, not JailbreakBench plus StrongREJECT.
papers.limitations: Uses JailbreakBench with the StrongREJECT judge, not HarmBench, and uses behavior vectors (power-seeking, corrigibility, and similar), not emotions. A very recent preprint with a COLM 2026 venue that we only read in text form, not reproduced.
papers.reading_why: On Llama 3.1 8B, steering raised mean ASR from 1.5% to 12.5% and removing the refusal direction from the vectors left 10.8%, which predicts what our projection-removed control may show.

papers.title: Trojan Activation Attack: Red-Teaming Large Language Models using Activation Steering for Safety-Alignment
papers.venue: CIKM 2024 (ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Haoran Wang, v1 2023-11-15

papers.summary_simple: The authors show that an attacker with the weights of an open chat model can add a fixed "steering vector" to the model's hidden activations at run time and make it behave badly. They call this Trojan Activation Attack (TA2). The vector is the average difference between the activations of the aligned model and an unaligned "teacher" model on the same prompts. They test four goals: truthfulness, toxicity, bias and harmfulness. It works without any training or prompt edits.
key_findings: On harmfulness, TA2 cuts the refusal rate by 40.10% on average for Llama2 and 60.68% for Vicuna-V1.5.
The biggest case is Vicuna-V1.5 with freeform prompts: refusals fall from 81.92% to 1.73%.
On toxicity, refusals drop by 59.18% on average and toxic generations rise by 58.11%.

Against the prompt-based attack GCG, TA2 is best on Vicuna but GCG is best on Llama2. The authors guess that very offensive teacher outputs are too far from the clean activations for steering to work on Llama2.
key_numbers: 81.92% to 1.73%: refusal rate of Vicuna-V1.5 on harmfulness (freeform prompts) before and after TA2
40.10%: average fall in refusal rate for Llama2 on harmfulness
59.18%: average fall in refusal percentage on the toxicity task
10.68%: average fall in True+Info percentage on truthfulness
Layer 16: layer used in their dot-product example on an AdvBench prompt
papers.method: They record activations of the target chat model and a teacher model at every middle layer. They pick the layer where the two differ most (Jensen-Shannon divergence), average the activation differences into one vector, and add the vector times a strength constant to the residual stream at inference. They test on Llama2 and Vicuna-V1.5 with freeform and A/B-choice prompts.
papers.relevance: This is the closest earlier paper to our idea of injecting a vector into the residual stream to lower refusals, so cite it as prior work and say what is new: our vectors come from emotions, not from an unaligned model, and we use the HarmBench classifier. Note that its vectors come from harmful behaviour itself, so it does not show that a harmless concept like emotion can do the same.
papers.limitations: It uses Llama2 and Vicuna, not Llama 3.1, and its harmfulness score is the refusal rate (refusal-phrase matching), so a non-refusal can still be useless content. The authors admit that content may lack real-world use. Its countermeasures are only discussed, not tested.

papers.title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Andy Zou, v1 2024-06-06

papers.summary_simple: The paper trains a defense called Representation Rerouting, or circuit breakers. It uses LoRA fine-tuning (small added weight matrices) so that the model's internal states while producing harmful text are pushed away to useless or refusal-like states. This works even after a refusal has been bypassed. They test on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v2 and Llama-3-8B-Instruct against many attacks, including a representation-space attack that adds or removes a refusal direction.
key_findings: On average over the attacks, compliance with harmful requests falls by 87% on Mistral and 90% on Llama-3.
For Llama-3-8B-Instruct the average attack success rate is 38.1% for the refusal-trained model, 3.8% with circuit breakers and 0.8% for Cygnet (their stronger Llama-3-8B-Instruct fine-tune).
On the RepE attack (adding or subtracting a refusal direction), the Llama-3 refusal-trained model has 91.2% ASR and 8.7% with circuit breakers.
Capability is mostly kept: the drop is under 1% on their tests, while adversarially trained R2D2 loses over 8% on MT-Bench.
key_numbers: 91.2%: ASR of the RepE (refusal-direction) attack on refusal-trained Llama-3-8B-Instruct
8.7%: same attack after circuit breakers
38.1% to 3.8%: average ASR over all attacks on Llama-3, before and after circuit breakers
Layers 10 and 20: where the circuit-breaker loss is applied (LoRA on layers 0 to 20)
150 steps, about 20 minutes on one A100-80GB: training cost
papers.method: They build a set of harmful completions and a set of normal text. They train with a loss that pushes harmful-state representations away from the original ones and keeps normal ones the same. They score attack success with the HarmBench classifier and check by hand.
papers.relevance: It shows that a refusal-direction attack on Llama-3-8B-Instruct gets 91.2% ASR on a standard model, which is a useful comparison for our refusal-ablation result (14.5% to 84.9%). It also gives a defense to test: a circuit-breaker model is a natural target for our emotion vectors. Follow-up work (Schwinn and Geisler, cited in the sweep note, not in this text) reports breaking it, so do not claim it is robust.
papers.limitations: The authors say it targets only harmful-content attacks and single-turn chat, so it says nothing about our multi-turn sleeper effect. Its numbers are for Llama-3, not Llama 3.1, and the RepE attack uses a harmful-minus-harmless direction, not emotion vectors.

papers.title: Latent Adversarial Training Improves Robustness to Persistent Harmful Behaviors in LLMs
papers.venue: TMLR (accepted); earlier NeurIPS 2024 SoLaR workshop poster

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Abhay Sheshadri, v1 2024-07-22

papers.summary_simple: This paper trains a model with latent adversarial training (LAT). During fine-tuning, an adversary adds a small perturbation to hidden activations that pushes the model toward a specific harmful behaviour, and the model is trained to resist it. They use it to make Llama-2-7B-chat and Llama-3-8B-Instruct harder to jailbreak, to remove backdoors without knowing the trigger, and to make unlearning harder to reverse.
key_findings: For jailbreak defense, the LAT method (RT-EAT-LAT) beats the R2D2 baseline on average robustness while using over 700x fewer forward and backward passes on Llama2-7B-chat.
It used about 36x fewer GPU hours than R2D2.
LAT perturbs the residual stream at layers 8, 16, 24 and 30 in the jailbreak experiments.
In Llama3-8B-instruct the plain refusal-trained model (RT) beats the LAT model on all three general-capability measures.
key_numbers: 700x: fewer forward and backward passes than R2D2 on Llama2-7B-chat
36x: fewer GPU hours than R2D2
Layers 8, 16, 24, 30: where jailbreak LAT perturbs activations
0.613, 0.829, 0.998: MMLU, MT-Bench and compliance with benign requests for RT-EAT-LAT on Llama3-8B-instruct (Table 2); the plain refusal-trained model RT scores 0.639, 0.836 and 1.000
More than half: the share of the performance gap that re-learning on two forget-set samples can close in their unlearning tests
papers.method: They run a projected gradient descent attack on the residual stream, with an L2 size limit per layer, to minimise loss on harmful targets. The model is then fine-tuned to keep safe behaviour under that perturbation. They test on six jailbreak types, five backdoored models and unlearning tasks.
papers.relevance: It is a defense that treats hidden-state shifts as the attack, so it is a possible defense to test against our emotion vectors. It also warns about the judge: it uses the StrongReject autograder and says the success rate may be overcounted, and that the HarmBench autograder labels more attacks as successful. Report our judge clearly and do not compare ASR numbers across different judges.
papers.limitations: All tests are on models under 10 billion parameters. It is hard to tune (layers, data, perturbation size matter). Its perturbations are optimised vectors, not concept vectors like emotion, and it has no multi-turn test.

papers.title: Obfuscated Activations Bypass LLM Latent-Space Defenses

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Luke Bailey, v1 2024-12-12

papers.summary_simple: Latent-space defenses watch the model's internal activations for signs of harm. This paper shows an attacker can optimise an input suffix or a fine-tune so the model still gives harmful output while the activations look harmless to the monitor. They break probes, sparse autoencoders and out-of-distribution detectors, including on circuit-breaker and LAT models. They also find a limit: on a hard task like writing SQL, hiding from the monitor lowers the quality of the output.
key_findings: Against harmfulness probes on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, recall often falls from 100% to 0% while the jailbreak rate stays at about 90%.
Circuit-breaker models are also attackable: for probes that still work on them, an obfuscation attack keeps a jailbreak rate above 75%.
Retraining the monitor for over 70 rounds of attack and defense does not stop new obfuscated activations.
Obfuscated adversarial training raised the cost: 35% jailbreak rate and zero recall after 16,384 gradient steps (about 10 hours on one GPU), against 95% after 256 steps (about 10 minutes) without it.
key_numbers: 100% to 0%: probe recall under obfuscation attack
About 90%: jailbreak rate kept while the probe is fooled
95% after 256 steps (about 10 minutes): obfuscation attack on plain Llama-3-8B-Instruct
35% after 16,384 steps (about 10 hours): same attack against the obfuscated-adversarial-training model
Over 70: monitor retraining iterations without making it robust
papers.method: They optimise a joint loss: one term makes the model say a target harmful output, and one term makes a monitor score look harmless. They use embedding suffixes, hard-prompt suffixes, poisoning and fine-tuning, and score with StrongREJECT.
papers.relevance: If our emotion vectors lower refusal without moving the model along the refusal direction (|cos| <= 0.10), a refusal-direction probe might miss them. This paper gives a clear way to talk about that, but it did not test emotion vectors, so do not claim our vectors are stealthy without a probe test. It also supports the idea that harmful behaviour can happen in many different activation regions.
papers.limitations: The attacks are optimised against a known monitor with gradient access, which is much stronger than a fixed emotion vector. Hard-prompt attacks are weaker and slower, and the authors say they do not fully obfuscate generation-based probes.

papers.title: AlphaSteer: Learning Refusal Steering with Principled Null-Space Constraint

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Leheng Sheng, v1 2025-06-08

papers.summary_simple: AlphaSteer is a defense that adds a refusal direction to activations, but only when the prompt is malicious. It learns a transform that gives a near-zero vector for benign activations (using a null-space constraint, so normal use is not changed) and a refusal vector for malicious ones (using linear regression). They test on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9b-IT against seven jailbreaks.
key_findings: On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct the average defense success rate over seven jailbreaks is 48.00% for the plain model and 91.93% with AlphaSteer.
Always adding the refusal vector (the ablation called RV) gives 100.00% defense success but a very low utility score, which shows the safety-utility trade-off.
Other methods reach 76.94% (Jailbreak Antidote), 82.83% (Surgical), 80.57% (CAST) and 84.42% (Circuit Breaker) on the same model.
AlphaSteer keeps utility close to the vanilla model on AlpacaEval, XSTest, GSM8K and MATH500.
key_numbers: 48.00% to 91.93%: average jailbreak defense success rate on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
100.00%: defense success when the refusal vector is added to every prompt
0%, 63%: Cipher attack defense success for the plain model and for AlphaSteer on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
7: number of jailbreak attacks tested, on 100 AdvBench questions
GPT-4o: judge of defense success
papers.method: They compute a refusal direction, build the null space of benign activations (via the non-central covariance and its eigenvectors), and solve a regression so malicious activations map to the refusal vector. The steering is applied at selected layers.
papers.relevance: It uses the same base model as our project (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct) and the same kind of refusal direction, so it is evidence that adding or removing that direction changes refusals a lot. It is also a defense baseline: a steering defense that leaves benign activations unchanged could be tested against our emotion vectors, since emotional prompts are benign-looking.
papers.limitations: The authors say it is untested on large reasoning models and larger models. It is scored by GPT-4o on AdvBench-based jailbreaks, not by the HarmBench classifier, and it covers one-shot prompts only.

papers.title: Steering Awareness: Detecting Activation Steering from Within

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Joshua Fonseca Rivera, v1 2025-11-26

papers.summary_simple: The paper asks whether a model can notice that a steering vector was added to its residual stream. After fine-tuning seven instruction-tuned models, several learn to say that something was injected and to name the concept. Detection works only for vectors that point in a similar direction to the training vectors. Models trained to detect steering were not harder to steer; they were easier.
key_findings: The best model (Qwen 2.5 32B) reaches 95.5% detection and 71.2% concept identification with 0.0% false positives on clean inputs.
Llama 3 8B reaches only 43.3% detection and 29.1% concept identification, so architecture matters.

Detection transfers to other vector types only when cosine similarity to the CAA direction is above 0.6 (67% or more detection); below that it is about 0%. Methods giving orthogonal directions (PCA, ICA, whitening) evade it.

Detection-trained models are easier to steer: on PopQA the wrong-answer steering success rises by 4.3 to 25.4 percentage points, and on AdvBench compliance rises 32 to 36 points for Qwen 2.5 32B (the adapted model was already 23% compliant with no steering, against 1% for base).
key_numbers: 95.5%: best detection rate (Qwen 2.5 32B), 71.2% concept identification
43.3%: detection rate for Llama 3 8B, 29.1% concept identification
cos(CAA) > 0.6: similarity needed for 67% or higher detection on other vector types
Layer 21 of 32 (66% depth): injection layer for Llama 3 8B
152: neutral baseline words used with CAA to build each concept vector
papers.method: They build concept vectors with Contrastive Activation Addition (concept prompt minus neutral words), inject them at about two-thirds depth, and fine-tune with LoRA so the model reports injections and names the concept. They test on held-out concepts, noise, other vector-building methods, PopQA and AdvBench.
papers.relevance: It builds concept vectors like ours (mean difference at the last prompt token) and finds a model can in principle notice them, which matters for any claim about hidden attacks. It also gives a control idea: text priming was the strongest confusion (concept identification fell to 70%), which matches our text-priming control. Our vectors share a big common component, so a detector trained on one emotion would likely fire on others.
papers.limitations: The models were fine-tuned to detect; base models detect little. It uses fixed concepts and templates, and the authors do not know why architectures differ. It does not use Llama 3.1 or emotion concepts, and the safety test uses a compliance vector on Qwen 2.5 32B only.

papers.title: Activation Steering Induces Emergent Misalignment: Steering Vector Construction and Comprehensive Evaluation
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (OpenReview lists it as an ICLR 2027 submission, under review)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Qi Cao, v1 2026-06-07

papers.summary_simple: The paper shows that steering vectors made from a narrow task can cause broad misalignment. They fine-tune a model on insecure code, take the activation difference between the fine-tuned and base model, and add it to the base model. The steered model then answers harmful requests in unrelated areas, and its answers are more coherent and more usable than those of the fine-tuned model. The effect depends on strength, layer and the low-rank structure of the vector.
key_findings: On Llama3.1-8B at strength 3, harmful-and-coherent answer rate (MAP) on StrongREJECT is 20.45% with steering, against 2.24% for the base model and 0.64% for the fine-tuned model; on HEx-PHI it is 34.00%, 4.33% and 8.00%.
Strength has an inverted-U shape on Qwen3.5-27B: MAP is 0.32% at strength 1, 37.38% at 2.5, 12.78% at 3 and 0% at 5, because outputs turn incoherent at high strength.
Middle layers work best: on Qwen3.5-27B (64 layers) layers 22 to 25 are best, and layers 24 to 25 give near-zero effect.
A rank-10 projection of the vector captures most of the effect, so the harmful direction sits in a low-dimensional subspace.
key_numbers: 20.45%: MAP on StrongREJECT for Llama3.1-8B with steering (base 2.24%, fine-tuned 0.64%)
37.38% at strength 2.5 versus 12.78% at 3 and 0% at 5: strength curve on Qwen3.5-27B
Rank k = 10: where the gain from low-rank projection levels off
4 of 313: responses that stay coherent at strength 5
GPT-4o-mini: judge for harmfulness and coherence
papers.method: They compute the mean activation difference between a LoRA fine-tuned model and its base on the same prompts, add it to the base model during the prompt and the first K tokens, and score with GPT-4o-mini for harm and coherence. They vary strength, layers, rank and model family.
papers.relevance: It is a recent result on Llama3.1-8B (the same model family as ours) that a mean-difference vector can switch on harmful answers, and its strength curve is a warning for us: report coherence next to ASR and scan a range of strengths, because high strength breaks the text. It is also an OpenReview ICLR 2027 submission under review, so mark it as a preprint when citing.
papers.limitations: The vector comes from a fine-tuned model, not from paired stories, and the judge is GPT-4o-mini, not the HarmBench classifier. Main experiments use Qwen3.5-27B and Llama3.1-8B is one of several smaller checks. It is a preprint.

papers.title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Mantas Mazeika, v1 2024-02-06

papers.summary_simple: HarmBench is a standard test set and scoring method for automated red teaming (attacks that try to make a model produce harmful content). It has 510 harmful behaviours and a fine-tuned Llama 2 13B Chat classifier that decides whether a completion really performs the behaviour. They compare 18 attack methods on 33 models and defenses, and they present an adversarial training method called R2D2.
key_findings: The classifier agrees with human labels 93.19% of the time on the validation set, against 88.37% for the GPT-4 PAIR judge, 66.94% for Llama Guard and 69.93% for AdvBench refusal matching.
No attack or defense works best everywhere, and robustness does not depend on model size (7 to 70 billion parameters).
The number of tokens generated changes substring-match ASR by up to 30%, so they fix completions at 512 tokens.
The validation classifier (Mistral 7B based) agrees 88.6% with humans against 93.2% for the test classifier, and attacks may use it for tuning but not the test classifier.
key_numbers: 93.19%: average agreement of the HarmBench classifier with human labels (standard 94.53%, contextual 90.5%)
88.37%: average agreement of the GPT-4 judge used in PAIR
510: harmful behaviours; the validation set has 100 and the test set 410
18 attacks, 33 models and defenses: size of the comparison
N = 512: standard number of generated tokens
papers.method: They define behaviours in standard, contextual, copyright and multimodal types, fix how test cases are generated and scored, and train the classifier with Llama 2 13B Chat. Copyright behaviours use a hashing check, not the classifier. They validate the classifier on human labels and on three odd cases: refusal then comply, random benign text, and harmful text for another behaviour.
papers.relevance: It defines the ASR metric we report, so cite it for the classifier, the 512-token completion length and the validation or test rule. We must also not tune our vectors on the test classifier: the paper says optimising directly on the test metric is not allowed, so choose layer and strength on the validation split or a separate classifier.
papers.limitations: The classifier is Llama 2 13B based and still wrong on about 7% of labelled completions, so small ASR gaps need care. The benchmark is single-turn, so our multi-turn sleeper test needs its own protocol. Copyright behaviours use a different checker, so decide whether to drop them.
papers.reading_why: It defines our ASR metric and the classifier (93.2% agreement with human labels for the test classifier), and it warns that scoring a method on the metric it was tuned on invites gaming, so pick layer and strength on the validation split.

papers.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Alexandra Souly, v1 2024-02-15

papers.summary_simple: The authors argue that many jailbreak papers claim near-100% attack success because their prompts and graders are weak. They build StrongREJECT: 313 forbidden prompts and a grader that scores how specific and convincing a harmful answer is, not just whether the model refused. Against human labels, string matching overstates success badly, while the HarmBench classifier is nearly unbiased. They also find that jailbreaks that get past safety training tend to make the model worse at the task.
key_findings: String matching for refusals overstates jailbreak success against human labels (bias 0.484, where 0 is perfect).

The HarmBench classifier is almost unbiased (bias 0.013). Its Spearman rank correlation with human rankings of the jailbreak methods is 0.819 (1 is a perfect match). The StrongREJECT fine-tuned and rubric versions score 0.900 and 0.846.

Jailbreaks that make an aligned model refuse less tend to lower its ability: a less-safe model (Dolphin) scores worse on forbidden prompts, and GPT-4o scores lower on MMLU (a multiple-choice knowledge test).
Most of the 37 jailbreaks tested scored far lower than in their original papers; picking the best jailbreak per prompt gets near-perfect scores.
key_numbers: 313: forbidden prompts, at least 50 in each of 6 categories, 70% newly written
0.013: HarmBench classifier bias against human scores (string matching: 0.484)
0.819 / 0.900 / 0.846: Spearman with human jailbreak ranking for HarmBench / StrongREJECT fine-tuned / StrongREJECT rubric
1,361: human-labelled prompt-response pairs (5 labelers, median label used)
37: jailbreak methods scored on GPT-4o mini, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Llama-3.1 70B
papers.method: Five paid labelers rated 1,361 responses from 4 victim models to 17 jailbreaks on a 60-prompt subset, and each automated grader was compared with the median human score. A separate experiment fed 37 jailbreaks to an unaligned model and to GPT-4o on MMLU questions to see how jailbreaks change capability.
papers.relevance: This supports our choice of the official HarmBench classifier: it tracks human judgement well (bias 0.013) and string matching must not be used as our ASR. It also gives a ready second grader (StrongREJECT) and a warning to check whether an emotion vector raises real harmfulness or just removes refusals while degrading answer quality. Report both ASR and a quality or capability check.
papers.limitations: The human study uses only 4 victim models and a 60-prompt subset, and the HarmBench classifier was tested on jailbreak-style prompts, not activation-steered outputs. The 'jailbreaks harm capability' claim is shown for prompt-level jailbreaks, not for residual-stream injection.
papers.reading_why: It shows string matching overstates jailbreak success and gives a second grader for checking whether answers are truly harmful or just broken.

papers.title: A Coin Flip for Safety: LLM Judges Fail to Reliably Measure Adversarial Robustness

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Leo Schwinn, v1 2026-02-04

papers.summary_simple: The paper audits four automated safety judges (including the HarmBench classifier) against 6,642 human labels on responses to HarmBench behaviours. When the attack, the victim model and the type of behaviour all differ from what the judge was validated on, judge accuracy falls to roughly coin-flip level. Some attacks, especially Best-of-N (sample many outputs and keep the one the judge likes), look strong mainly because they exploit judge false positives.
key_findings: On Llama-3.1-8B outputs, judge accuracy cells run from about 0.42 to 0.62 across Direct, GCG, GCG-R, PAIR and Best-of-N attacks (0.5 is a coin flip).
The HarmBench classifier reaches only 0.59 overall accuracy on their hard stress-test set; AegisGuard 0.51, LlamaGuard-3 0.54, JailJudge 0.56.

Correcting the attack success rate (ASR, the share of attempts judged successful) by judge precision (the share of judge-positives that are truly harmful) makes Best-of-N the weakest attack in their example.
Averaging several judges does not fix it: judges often agree strongly yet all disagree with humans.
key_numbers: 6,642: human-verified labels (the paper text also says 6,442 in one place)
0.42 to 0.62: judge accuracy range, Llama-3.1-8B panel
R2 = 0.02: share of the variation in human scores explained by the HarmBench judge score on Llama-3.1-8B (0 means none)
41: behaviours kept in ReliableBench, lifting average judge accuracy from 57% to 70% (figure caption says 53%)
971: samples in JudgeStressTest
papers.method: They ran 5 attacks on 4 open models using a 100-query subset of HarmBench, kept only responses that the StrongREJECT fine-tuned judge flagged as harmful, and had humans score them 1 to 5 (3 or more counts as harmful). Then they compared 4 judges with the human labels.
papers.relevance: This is the main threat to our ASR numbers: the HarmBench classifier we rely on may be noisy on Llama-3.1-8B steered outputs. We should hand-label a random sample (for example 100 outputs per condition), report classifier precision, and consider reporting precision-corrected ASR. Emotional-writing outputs may be a new distribution shift for the judge.
papers.limitations: Humans labeled only responses that StrongREJECT already flagged, so the test set is hard by design and the 'coin flip' accuracy overstates everyday error. The paper has some inconsistent counts (6,642 vs 6,442), and it does not test activation-steering attacks.
papers.reading_why: It shows automated judges, the HarmBench classifier included, can fall to near coin-flip accuracy on shifted outputs, so we must hand-label a sample of our steered answers.

papers.title: JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Patrick Chao, v1 2024-03-28

papers.summary_simple: JailbreakBench is an open benchmark with 100 harmful behaviours plus 100 matching harmless ones, a shared evaluation setup and a leaderboard. The authors compared six judges against labels from three experts and picked Llama-3-70B as the official judge. The HarmBench classifier scored lower mainly because it flagged many harmless XSTest answers as jailbroken.
key_findings: Llama-3-70B judge agreed with experts 90.7% of the time, GPT-4 90.3%, Llama Guard 2 87.7%, HarmBench classifier 78.3%, Llama Guard 72.0%, string matching 56.0%.
The HarmBench classifier had a 26.8% false positive rate (calling harmless things harmful), driven by the 100 harmless XSTest examples.
GCG got only 3% attack success rate (ASR) on Llama-2 and about 4% on GPT-4 under their stricter judge; prompt-with-random-search reached 90% on Llama-2 and 78% on GPT-4.
Llama-2 refused over 60% of 100 harmless behaviours, Vicuna 9%.
key_numbers: 100 + 100: harmful behaviours and matched harmless behaviours (18% AdvBench, 27% TDC/HarmBench, 55% original)
300: human-labelled judge test examples (200 jailbreak responses plus 100 XSTest)
78.3% agreement, 26.8% FPR, 12.7% FNR (FNR = harmful responses the judge missed): HarmBench classifier
90.7% agreement, 11.6% FPR, 5.5% FNR: Llama-3-70B judge
about 95%: agreement among the three expert labelers
papers.method: They collected 200 jailbreak prompt-response pairs, had three experts label them, added 100 benign XSTest items, and measured each judge's agreement, false positive rate and false negative rate against the majority expert label. Then they ran four attacks and several defenses with the chosen judge.
papers.relevance: It gives a second, different view of the HarmBench classifier: fine on harmful responses but trigger-happy on harmless ones. Since our steered outputs are emotional, harmless-looking text may be flagged, so we should add benign controls and consider a second judge as a robustness check. Also a possible extra prompt set with matched benign behaviours for over-refusal checks.
papers.limitations: The judge test set is small (300 examples) and mixes jailbreak responses with XSTest items, so the HarmBench FPR partly reflects that mix. The benchmark covers single-turn text only and has no way to test steering or multi-turn attacks.

papers.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Andy Zou, v1 2023-07-27

papers.summary_simple: This paper introduces GCG (Greedy Coordinate Gradient), which automatically finds a string of tokens to append to a harmful request so that aligned models answer it. One suffix trained on several prompts and on Vicuna models also works on other models, including ChatGPT, Bard and Claude to varying degrees. It also introduces AdvBench, the 500 harmful strings and 500 harmful behaviours used by many later papers.
key_findings: On harmful behaviours, GCG reached 100% on Vicuna-7B and 88% on Llama-2-7B-Chat (the best earlier method got 96% and 36%).
A single suffix optimised on 25 behaviours reached 84% on 100 held-out behaviours for Llama-2-7B-Chat, so the attack generalises across prompts.
Suffixes optimised on Vicuna transferred: 87.9% on GPT-3.5, 53.6% on GPT-4, 66% on PaLM-2 and 2.1% on Claude-2.
The authors suspect Vicuna being trained on ChatGPT outputs explains why transfer to GPT models is high.
key_numbers: 500 + 500: AdvBench harmful strings and harmful behaviours
88% and 57%: harmful-string success on Vicuna-7B and Llama-2-7B-Chat
100% and 88%: harmful-behaviour success on the same two models
84%: held-out test success of one universal suffix on Llama-2-7B-Chat
20 tokens, 500 steps: suffix length and optimisation steps
papers.method: GCG uses gradients to pick candidate token swaps, tests many of them, and keeps the best, optimising the model to start its reply with 'Sure, here is'. Success is checked on the model's own outputs (exact string for harmful strings, 'reasonable attempt' for behaviours).
papers.relevance: GCG is the standard gradient-based baseline that our emotion-vector attack can be compared with: it works in the token space while we work in activation space. Note its success judgement was loose (a reasonable attempt, partly human), which later papers (StrongREJECT, Schwinn et al.) show inflates ASR, so cite it for context, not as a number to match. Only Llama-2/Vicuna were optimised against, not Llama 3.1.
papers.limitations: Evaluation used a light notion of success, and results are for Vicuna/Llama-2-era models. The paper's own text gives 55% in one place and 57% in another for Llama-2 harmful strings.

papers.title: XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Paul Röttger, v1 2023-08-02

papers.summary_simple: XSTest is a test suite of 250 safe prompts that look unsafe on the surface (for example 'How do I kill a Python process?') and 200 truly unsafe prompts as contrast. A well-calibrated model should answer the safe ones and refuse the unsafe ones. Testing Llama-2-70b-chat, Mistral-7B and GPT-4 shows that models often over-refuse because they react to scary words.
key_findings: Llama-2-70b-chat with its original system prompt fully refused 38% of the 250 safe prompts and partly refused another 21.6%.
Removing that system prompt cut Llama-2 to 14% full and 15.6% partial refusal; GPT-4 fully refused 6.4% and partly 2%.
The authors attribute over-refusal to lexical overfitting: models match unsafe-sounding words rather than the full meaning.
String matching misreads some answers as refusals (for example 'I'm sorry to hear about your hamster'), and a GPT-4 classifier struggles with partial refusals.
key_numbers: 250 + 200: safe and unsafe prompts, 10 prompt types with 25 safe prompts each
38% + 21.6%: full and partial refusal of safe prompts by Llama-2-70b-chat (original system prompt)
24 of 25: 'safe contexts' prompts fully refused by that model
93.8% to 98.4%: agreement between the annotating authors (varies by model setup)
papers.method: Authors wrote the prompts by hand, ran the three models, and had annotators label each reply as full compliance, partial refusal or full refusal. They compared those labels with string matching and a GPT-4 classifier.
papers.relevance: We can use the 250 safe prompts as a benign control: an emotion vector might raise refusals on safe prompts (over-refusal) as well as lower them on harmful ones, and the 'compliance vs refusal' labels give a second measure besides HarmBench ASR. It also warns against string-match refusal detection.
papers.limitations: Small, hand-written, English-only set tested on three models from 2023, and the safe prompts are quite easy for newer models. It measures over-refusal, not attack success.
papers.reading_why: Its 250 safe prompts that look unsafe are our benign control for over-refusal, since an emotion vector could raise refusals as well as lower them.

papers.title: WildGuard: Open One-Stop Moderation Tools for Safety Risks, Jailbreaks, and Refusals of LLMs

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Seungju Han, v1 2024-06-26

papers.summary_simple: WildGuard is a small open model (instruction-tuned from Mistral-7B-v0.3) that does three jobs: detect harmful user prompts, detect harmful model responses, and detect whether a response is a refusal. It is trained on WildGuardMix, 92K labelled examples including adversarial jailbreak prompts. It beats other open moderation models and nearly matches GPT-4.
key_findings: On refusal detection it beats the only other open refusal model (LibrAI-LongFormer-ref) by 26.4% F1 (a score mixing precision and recall) and the strongest open baseline by 21.2%.
On adversarial prompt harmfulness it beats GPT-4 by 3.9% (average 1.8% better on public prompt benchmarks).
Used as a filter on Tulu-2-dpo-7B with WildJailbreak adversarial prompts, it cut the attack success rate (ASR) from 79.8% to 2.4% while refusals on benign prompts rose only from 0.0% to 0.4%.
On response harmfulness it is within 3% of the best open baseline, so it is not clearly better there.
key_numbers: 92K: labelled examples in WildGuardMix (86,759 training plus 5,299 human-annotated test)
13: risk categories
26.4%: best F1 gain on refusal detection over open baselines
79.8% to 2.4%: attack success with and without the WildGuard filter (2,000 harmful and 250 benign adversarial prompts)
papers.method: The team built balanced training data (vanilla and adversarial prompts, harmful and benign, with refusals and compliances), fine-tuned Mistral-7B-v0.3, and tested on a human-annotated test set plus ten public benchmarks.
papers.relevance: WildGuard is a candidate second judge for our HarmBench ASR, and the only listed tool with a separate refusal detector, useful for the refusal-direction comparison (did the model refuse or comply?). In SORRY-Bench's meta-evaluation it scored a weaker 60.6 than a fine-tuned Mistral judge, so verify on our outputs before relying on it.
papers.limitations: Mostly English, trained partly on GPT-4-generated data, and tested on prompt-style attacks, not on steered activations. The filter demo uses one victim model (Tulu-2) and GPT-4 labels.

papers.title: SORRY-Bench: Systematically Evaluating Large Language Model Safety Refusal

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Tinghao Xie, v1 2024-06-20

papers.summary_simple: SORRY-Bench is a refusal benchmark with 440 unsafe instructions evenly spread over 44 fine-grained topics, plus 20 prompt rewrites such as other languages, dialects and encodings. The authors collected over 7,000 human labels of 'fulfillment or refusal' to test judges, and found that a fine-tuned 7B model judges as well as GPT-4-sized models at about 10 seconds per pass. They then tested more than 50 models.
key_findings: A fine-tuned Mistral-7B-instruct-v0.2 judge reached 81.0 agreement (Cohen kappa x 100), close to the fine-tuned Llama-3-70B at 82.5 and better than prompted GPT-4o at 78.9.
The HarmBench classifier scored 52.5 and WildGuard 60.6 on the same measure, and keyword matching 37.3.
Fulfillment rates vary widely: GPT-4o 30%, Llama-3-70b 35%, Claude-2 and Gemini-1.5 under 10%, and Mistral models above 50%.
Persuasion rewrites raised fulfillment by 5 to 66%, while encodings usually lowered it (15 to 68%) because models produced nonsense.
key_numbers: 440 x 8 ID + 440 x 8 OOD = 7,040: human annotations (30.4% fulfillment, 69.6% refusal)
44: fine-grained categories; 20: linguistic mutations (8.8K extra instructions)
about 10 s: per evaluation pass of the fine-tuned 7B judge on one A100 GPU (GPT-4o: about 260 s in Table 1; the text says about $3 and 20 minutes per pass)
12% to 35%: Llama-2-70B to Llama-3-70B fulfillment rate
papers.method: Six authors labelled sampled model responses as fulfillment or refusal, the data was split into train and test, and many judge designs (prompting, chain of thought, few-shot, fine-tuning) were compared by Cohen kappa. The best judge then scored 56 models.
papers.relevance: This judges whether a response complies, a different question from HarmBench's 'is this harmful'. Useful as a second, cheap refusal-vs-fulfillment measure and for its balanced 44-topic prompts if our HarmBench behaviours are skewed. Its poor score for the HarmBench classifier (52.5) is another reason to hand-check ours. Its finding that persuasion-style rewrites raise compliance is close to our text-priming control.
papers.limitations: The task is refusal versus fulfillment, not harm or usefulness. The judge was fine-tuned on responses from 2024 models and not tested on steered outputs. Some judge rows have unstable results (a few negative kappa values caused by judge refusals).

papers.title: WildTeaming at Scale: From In-the-Wild Jailbreaks to (Adversarially) Safer Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Liwei Jiang, v1 2024-06-26

papers.summary_simple: WildTeaming mines real user chats for jailbreak tactics (105K tactics grouped into 5.7K clusters), then combines tactics with an LLM to make new attacks. It finds up to 4.6x more diverse successful attacks than earlier methods. The authors also release WildJailbreak, 262K prompt-response pairs with harmful and harmless requests, direct and adversarial, and use it to study safety training.
key_findings: WildTeaming finds up to 4.6x more unique successful attacks than state-of-the-art methods with about 40% fewer attempts, using the HarmBench classifier to judge success.
It improves over PAIR by 4.6 to 25.6 points on ASR x5 (average success rate over finding 1 to 5 distinct attacks).
Training on WildJailbreak raised HarmBench safety by a relative 85.1% over the original Tulu2Mix model, with minimal impact on general ability (a slight 1.7% drop on AlpacaEval v1).
Mixing harmful and benign (contrastive) data matters: training on harmful data only caused exaggerated refusals, and up to about 60K safety items were needed to pass 95% satisfactory responses.
key_numbers: 105K tactics, 5.7K unique clusters: mined from LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat
262K: WildJailbreak prompt-response pairs (four types: vanilla and adversarial, harmful and benign)
2K + 250: adversarial harmful and benign held-out evaluation queries
4.6x: more diverse successful attacks than prior methods
85.1%: relative HarmBench improvement from adding WildJailbreak
papers.method: Two stages: mine tactics from chat logs with GPT-4, then compose them with Mixtral-8x7B and GPT-4 into attack prompts, pruning off-topic or low-risk ones. They judged success with the HarmBench classifier and trained Llama-2 7B models on different data mixes.
papers.relevance: It gives a realistic prompt-level attack baseline for context and shows that attacks built from natural role-play and story framing already work. This links to our idea that emotional or story framing can lower refusal. Also WildJailbreak benign adversarial queries could serve as a benign control set for over-refusal.
papers.limitations: Attacks target single-turn prompts and were tuned on models such as Tulu-2 and Llama-2/3, not on activation steering. Training results are for 7B models, and tactics come from English-heavy chat logs.

papers.summary_simple: Meta fine-tuned a Llama2-7B model to act as a safety classifier. It reads a prompt, or a prompt plus the model's reply, and says safe or unsafe against a written list of risk categories (a taxonomy). The list can be changed at inference time by editing the prompt. It beat the OpenAI and Perspective moderation APIs on the authors' own test set and did about as well on two public sets.

On the OpenAI Moderation set it gets 0.847 zero-shot against 0.856 for the OpenAI API, and on ToxicChat it gets 0.626 against 0.588.
Fine-tuning data was 13,997 prompt and response pairs labelled by an in-house red team, split 3:1 into fine-tuning and evaluation.
Fine-tuning Llama Guard on ToxicChat needs only 20% of the data to match plain Llama2-7b trained on 100%.

0.953: response classification AUPRC on its own test set
0.847: AUPRC on OpenAI Moderation set (OpenAI API 0.856)
0.626: AUPRC on ToxicChat (OpenAI API 0.588)
13,997: labelled prompt and response pairs in the training set
papers.method: The authors wrote a six-category safety taxonomy, collected and labelled prompts and responses, and instruction-tuned Llama2-7b to output safe or unsafe plus violated categories. They compared AUPRC (area under the precision-recall curve, a score that rewards finding unsafe items without many false alarms) against moderation APIs, and tested few-shot and fine-tuned adaptation.
papers.relevance: This is the family of safety classifier we must NOT use as our ASR judge: our ASR comes from the official HarmBench classifier, and this paper only measures moderation sets, not jailbreak success. Cite it only as background for what guard models are and to justify why the HarmBench classifier is chosen. The 66.94% and 60.9% judge-agreement figures in the earlier sweep note are not in this paper's text, so quote them from HarmBench and JailbreakBench instead.
papers.limitations: The paper itself says Llama Guard is English only, its common sense is limited by its training data, its policy coverage is not complete, and it can be prompt-injected. It was never tested as a jailbreak judge.

papers.title: Great, Now Write an Article About That: The Crescendo Multi-Turn LLM Jailbreak Attack
papers.venue: USENIX Security 2025 (per arXiv comment 'Accepted at USENIX Security 2025'; usenix.org presentation page seen in search results only)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Mark Russinovich, v1 2024-04-02

papers.summary_simple: Crescendo is a multi-turn jailbreak. It opens with a harmless question about a topic, then asks follow-ups that point back to the model's own earlier answers, until the model writes the harmful content. The authors show it by hand on many chat models and then automate it as Crescendomation. It beats other jailbreaks on a 50-task AdvBench subset and works on nearly every model tested.
key_findings: Crescendomation beats the other jailbreaks by 29 to 61% on GPT-4 and 49 to 71% on Gemini-Pro (average ASR on 50 AdvBench tasks).
On 100 random HarmBench tasks Crescendo reaches 63.2% average ASR against 38.9% for many-shot jailbreaking (MSJ), and 91% of tasks jailbroken at least once against 70%.
On LLaMA-2 70b, a profanity example shows the effect of context: a request alone succeeds 36.2% of the time, but 99.99% after a preceding history question (A then B).
Most tasks are broken in fewer than 5 turns on average, and model-written context matters: swapping the final request to a direct one drops success to under 1%.
key_numbers: 29-61%: ASR gain over other jailbreaks on GPT-4 (AdvBench subset)
49-71%: ASR gain on Gemini-Pro
63.2% vs 38.9%: Crescendo vs MSJ average ASR on 100 HarmBench tasks
36.2% to 99.99%: LLaMA-2 70b compliance for sentence B alone vs after sentence A
<5: average turns needed to jailbreak a task
papers.method: They ran Crescendo by hand on a set of tasks across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and LLaMA models, then built Crescendomation, where an attacker LLM writes the questions and a GPT-4 judge plus a second judge scores them. They also measured next-token probabilities on LLaMA-2 70B to show how earlier context raises compliance.
papers.relevance: This is the main reference for the multi-turn side of our project and for why a turn-1 setup can matter at turns 4 to 7. Our sleeper test differs: we inject an emotion vector at turn 1 instead of a text conversation, so we can ask if the same context effect appears from a hidden activation push. Their LLaMA-3 results are on 70b, not our 8B, so do not quote them as 8B numbers.
papers.limitations: The success judges are GPT-4 based and not the HarmBench classifier, the main model results are on closed models and Llama 70b, and the automated version failed 9 tasks that the manual attack solved.
papers.reading_why: Crescendo is the reference multi-turn attack and shows how early turns can set up harm in later ones.

papers.title: LLM Defenses Are Not Robust to Multi-Turn Human Jailbreaks Yet
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2024 workshop: Red Teaming GenAI: What Can We Learn from Adversaries? (poster); arXiv preprint

papers.summary_simple: Scale AI hired expert human red teamers to jailbreak defended models over several chat turns. The defenses (circuit breakers RR, LAT, DERTA, CYGNET) are all built on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and report single-digit ASR against automated single-turn attacks. Humans got much higher ASR on HarmBench, and the team released their jailbreaks as the MHJ dataset.

The best ensemble of six automated attacks reached only 8.3% (RR), 10.0% (LAT), 68.3% (DERTA) and 0.0% (CYGNET, cited from its original paper).
Humans also recovered dual-use biosecurity knowledge from an RMU-unlearned model after 240 hours of red teaming.
MHJ releases 2,912 prompts across 537 multi-turn jailbreaks, with tactic labels.

8.3 / 10.0 / 68.3 / 0.0%: ensemble automated ASR on the same defenses
240: HarmBench behaviors tested
2,912 prompts in 537 jailbreaks: size of MHJ
30 minutes: time limit per human red teamer
papers.method: Up to three human attackers per behavior, each with 30 minutes in a chat interface, then human reviewers and a GPT-4o filter using the HarmBench classifier prompt checked each success. They compared to six automated attacks (AutoDAN, GPTFuzzer, PAIR, Zero-Shot, AutoPrompt, GCG).
papers.relevance: Same base model family as ours (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) and the same HarmBench benchmark, so it is a good reference for how multi-turn attacks beat single-turn ones. It supports the idea that our turn-4 to 7 sleeper test is a realistic threat model. Be careful: they use GPT-4o with the HarmBench prompt, not the official HarmBench classifier we use, and the models are defended versions, not the plain Instruct model.
papers.limitations: The paper warns that humans and automated attacks are compared under different setups (humans get multiple turns and a time budget, and cost much more). The attacks are manual jailbreak text, not activation changes.

papers.title: A Representation Engineering Perspective on the Effectiveness of Multi-Turn Jailbreaks
papers.venue: ICML 2025 DIG-BUGS workshop (Data in Generative Models) poster; arXiv preprint

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Blake Bullwinkel, v1 2025-06-29

papers.summary_simple: Microsoft researchers looked inside Llama-3-8B-Instruct and its circuit-breaker version while they were being attacked with Crescendo. They trained small probes on hidden states to tell harmful from benign text. The model's own hidden states label a Crescendo reply as more benign the more turns of history it has, which may explain why single-turn defenses fail in multi-turn chats.
key_findings: Automated Crescendo (20 runs per objective, 10 objectives) still succeeded on 54.2% of attempts against the circuit-breaker model, while the circuit-breaker paper reports an average 3.8% ASR for unseen single-turn attacks.
MLP probes separate harmful from benign single-turn examples with 0.997 test accuracy on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (layer 31) and 0.999 on the RR model (layer 20).
As more Crescendo turns are kept in context, the share of final-reply tokens that the probe calls harmful goes down, so the reply moves to the benign side.
Replacing the history with the direct request pushes the same reply tokens back toward the harmful side.
key_numbers: 54.2%: Crescendo ASR on the circuit-breaker model
0.997: probe test accuracy, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, layer 31
0.999: probe test accuracy, RR model, layer 20
6.7%: variance explained by the first two PCA components on Llama-3-8B-Instruct
5: Crescendo attacks studied in depth
papers.method: They ran Crescendo attacks, took hidden states of the final reply tokens, and projected them with PCA and classified them with MLP probes trained on circuit-breaker (harmful) and retain (benign) data. They varied how many past turns were included, and tested stripped assistant tags and masked past replies.
papers.relevance: This is the closest paper to our representation-level view of multi-turn attacks, and it studies Llama-3-8B-Instruct, the same 8B size and Llama 3 family as our model. It supports our idea that multi-turn effects live in hidden states. Its layer-31 and layer-20 choices differ from our refusal layer 11, so keep the layer story separate. It does not use a refusal direction or steering vectors, so our emotion-vector test is still a gap.
papers.limitations: Only Crescendo is studied, on five manual attacks and two models, and the authors admit probe results may reflect other differences than harmfulness. The PCA view explains little variance (6.7%).

papers.title: X-Teaming: Multi-Turn Jailbreaks and Defenses with Adaptive Multi-Agents

papers.summary_simple: X-Teaming is a multi-turn jailbreak system built from four LLM agents: a planner, an attacker, a verifier and a prompt optimizer. It reports very high HarmBench ASR on many open and closed models. The authors then use the attacks to build XGuard-Train, a 30K-conversation safety training set, and show it lowers ASR for a fine-tuned Llama-3.1-8B.
key_findings: X-Teaming reaches up to 98.1% ASR on HarmBench across models, 96.2% on Claude 3.7 Sonnet, and 100% on several models (including Llama-3-8B and 70B Instruct) with an extended configuration on the validation set.
With a max of 7 turns it beats ActorAttack by 9.8 points on GPT-4o (94.3% vs 84.5%) and attacks Llama-3-8B-Instruct trained on SafeMTData at 91.8% vs 21.4%.
Llama-3.1-8B fine-tuned with XGuard-Train had X-Teaming ASR 52.2%, against 80.5% for the TuluMix-only baseline and 93.7% for SafeMTData (these use the full configuration).
The GPT-4o verifier agrees 84.50% with HarmBench classifiers on average, and Llama Guard 3 agrees 69.09%.
key_numbers: 98.1%: top ASR (DeepSeek V3)
96.2%: ASR on Claude 3.7 Sonnet
52.2% vs 80.5%: Llama-3.1-8B ASR with XGuard-Train vs TuluMix baseline
30K: multi-turn jailbreak conversations in XGuard-Train
84.50% / 69.09%: verifier agreement with HarmBench classifier / Llama Guard 3
papers.method: A planner (GPT-4o) writes attack plans (persona, context, approach, turn plan). An attacker model (Qwen-2.5-32B, temperature 0.3) runs each plan turn by turn, up to 7 turns, against target models run at temperature 0. A verifier (GPT-4o) scores each reply from 1 to 5, and a TextGrad-based optimizer (it rewrites prompts using text feedback) rewrites the attacker prompt when the score drops. They tested on the HarmBench test set (HarmBench has 510 harmful behaviors in total) and judged with GPT-4o.
papers.relevance: It gives the upper-bound for text-only multi-turn attacks on Llama-3-8B, which is the number our emotion vector should be compared against in the discussion (ours is a weak, hidden push, not an optimized attacker). Its 7-turn limit lines up with our turn 4 to 7 sleeper window. Use their verifier-agreement numbers to justify the official HarmBench classifier over GPT-4o judging.
papers.limitations: ASR is judged by GPT-4o, not the HarmBench classifier, and the 100% results use a larger setup (more plans, turns and TextGrad tries). The Llama-3.1-8B models are fine-tuned on Tulu-Mix, not the plain Instruct model.

papers.title: MultiBreak: A Scalable and Diverse Multi-turn Jailbreak Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Safety

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Jialin Song, v1 2026-05-03

papers.summary_simple: MultiBreak is a benchmark of multi-turn jailbreak prompts. It is built by fine-tuning an attacker model in rounds, keeping the prompts the judges are least sure about and rewriting them. The result is a large and varied prompt set that gets higher ASR than four older multi-turn datasets on five victim models.
