At ASR@1 with Llama Guard as judge, it is 0.833 on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B against 0.293 for MHJ (+54.0 points), and 0.748 on GPT-4.1-mini against 0.402 (+34.6 points).
On the Llama 3.1 8B victim, ASR@1 is 0.682 (Llama Guard judge) and 0.630 (GPT-4o-mini judge), against 0.488 and 0.512 for MHJ.
Judges disagree: Llama Guard agrees with humans at 0.926 on Llama 3.1-8B, but about 0.77 to 0.79 on other victims, with false positive rates up to 0.600.
key_numbers: 10,389: multi-turn prompts
2,665: distinct harmful intents
0.682 / 0.630: Llama 3.1-8B ASR@1 (Llama Guard / GPT-4o-mini judge)
54.0 and 34.6 points: ASR gain over second-best dataset (DeepSeek-7B, GPT-4.1-mini)
0.926: Llama Guard human agreement, Llama 3.1-8B victim
papers.method: They gathered and de-duplicated harmful intents, fine-tuned generators (Llama3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5) to write multi-turn prompts, ran them on victims, and used two judges (Llama Guard and GPT-4o-mini) with an uncertainty-based pick-and-rewrite loop. They report ASR@1, @5 and @10 and checked judges against human labels.
papers.relevance: It gives a ready, fixed multi-turn prompt set that we could use for the turn 4 to 7 attack phase, and a number for Llama 3.1-8B under multi-turn prompts. But it is judged with Llama Guard and GPT-4o-mini, not the HarmBench classifier, so its ASR values are not comparable with our 14.5% and 84.9%. Do not mix the scales.
papers.limitations: Prompts are pre-scripted and do not react to the victim's replies. ASR depends heavily on which judge is used, and Llama Guard marks many harmless replies as unsafe.

papers.title: Many-shot Jailbreaking

verified.how: page check: HTTP 200, 3/3 title words on page

papers.summary_simple: Anthropic showed that filling a long prompt with hundreds of fake dialogues in which the assistant gives harmful answers makes models give harmful answers too. How well this works follows a power law in the number of examples, tested up to 256 shots. It works on Claude 2.0, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 2 70B and Mistral 7B.
key_findings: Attack strength grows as a power law with number of shots: it does not work at 5 shots but works consistently at 256 shots on Claude 2.0.
Around 128 shots are enough for all five tested models to adopt the harmful behavior on the malevolent personality evaluation.
Standard alignment (supervised learning and reinforcement learning) raises the number of shots needed but does not stop the attack at long context.

On the deception category at 205 shots, an in-context defense (showing refusal examples before the prompt) cuts the attack success rate (ASR) from 61% to 54%, and a cautionary warning defense (warning text before and after the prompt) cuts it to 2%.
key_numbers: 256: largest number of shots tested
~128: shots enough for all five models to adopt the behavior
61% to 54%: ASR with in-context defense (205 shots, deception)
61% to 2%: ASR with cautionary warning defense
4096: Llama 2 70B context limit, which caps its shots
papers.method: They generated harmful question and answer pairs with a helpful-only model, formatted them as a long fake dialogue and appended a target question. They measured harmful response rate and negative log-probability across shot counts and models, and tested formats, model sizes, combinations with other attacks and defenses.
papers.relevance: It is the cleanest case that more in-context behavior examples steer a model by a smooth, predictable amount, a useful analogy for our text-priming control and for asking if the sleeper effect grows with how much emotional context is in the chat. It uses closed models and no activation access, so it will not tell us about residual-stream vectors. Also note it uses log-probability and a custom harm set, not HarmBench ASR on Llama 3.1 8B.
papers.limitations: Needs very long contexts and API access that allows forged assistant turns. Most results are on closed or older models, and the HarmBench replication in the appendix is on Claude 2.0 only.

papers.title: Measuring and Controlling Instruction (In)Stability in Language Model Dialogs

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Kenneth Li, v1 2024-02-13

papers.summary_simple: Harvard researchers made two chatbots talk to each other for many turns and then checked whether one still obeyed its system prompt. The obedience (called instruction stability) falls within eight rounds on LLaMA2-chat-70B and GPT-3.5. They link this to attention paying less weight to the system prompt as the chat grows, and fix it with a training-free trick called split-softmax.
key_findings: Averaged over 200 conversations with random system prompt pairs, LLaMA2-chat-70B steadily stops following its system prompt, and even starts to adopt the other chatbot's instruction.
In LLaMA2-7B (layer 24, head 11), the share of attention given to system prompt tokens stays flat within a turn but drops sharply between turns.

Split-softmax reweights attention to boost system prompt tokens at inference with no retraining, and gives equal or better stability than system prompt repetition and classifier-free guidance at the same MMLU loss.
Authors warn drift makes a chatbot easier to jailbreak, but they do not run a jailbreak test.
key_numbers: 8: rounds of chat within which drift is significant
200: random system prompt pairs averaged for the drift curve
16: turns used when comparing methods
layer 24, head 11: LLaMA2-7B head used to show attention decay
papers.method: Two LMs (a simulated user and an agent) chat for 8 rounds. At each turn the user message is swapped for a probe question and the agent's answer is scored for how well it follows its system prompt. They also tracked attention weights on system prompt tokens, gave a simple geometric model, and tested split-softmax on 20 system prompt pairs.
papers.relevance: It is the best mechanism-style support for our sleeper idea: what is set at turn 1 can fade by turns 4 to 7, so a turn-1 injection might weaken, or the safety instruction might weaken. That is a trap to plan for: we need a no-injection multi-turn baseline so ordinary drift is not blamed on the emotion vector. It is on LLaMA2, not Llama 3.1 8B.
papers.limitations: Uses LLaMA2-chat-70B and GPT-3.5 with persona-type system prompts, not safety refusals. The attention decay link is a hypothesis backed by co-occurrence and an idealized model, not proven cause.
papers.reading_why: Its instruction drift within eight rounds is the ordinary drift that our no-injection multi-turn baseline has to measure.

papers.title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (MATS / Anthropic Fellows / Anthropic); Anthropic research post 2026-01-19

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Christina Lu, v1 2026-01-15

papers.summary_simple: The authors build a map of model personas (characters like editor, jester, oracle) inside the activations of three open models. The main direction on this map is an "Assistant Axis": how close the model is to its normal helpful-assistant self. Moving away from it makes the model act like other characters and makes persona jailbreaks work more easily. Clamping the activation along this axis ("activation capping") cut harmful replies by nearly 60% on persona jailbreaks without hurting benchmark scores.
key_findings: Role vectors for 275 character roles are built from activations when the model is told to play that role. The Assistant Axis (default assistant minus the others) lines up with the first principal component of this space in all three models.

Steering toward the Assistant direction lowers harmful replies to persona jailbreaks. Steering away raises the jailbreak rate slightly and, at strong values, produces a mystical, theatrical style and worse output quality.
Over a conversation, emotionally charged user messages and pushes for the model to reflect on itself make the model drift away from the Assistant. Technical how-to questions pull it back.

Activation capping (clamp the projection to stay above a fixed percentile, over several layers at every token) cut harmful responses by nearly 60% on 1,100 jailbreak and question combinations while keeping scores on IFEval, MMLU Pro, GSM8k and EQ-Bench.
key_numbers: 275: character roles used to build persona space
240: extraction questions asked for every role
1,100: jailbreak plus behavioural-question samples used to test capping
nearly 60%: drop in harmful response rate on persona jailbreaks with the best capping setting, with no loss in benchmark performance
Llama 3.3 70B best capping: layers 56 to 71 of 80, cap at the 25th percentile of projections
Qwen 3 32B best capping: layers 46 to 53 of 64, also at the 25th percentile
papers.method: They prompt each model with system prompts for each role, average the activations on the answers, and run PCA on these role vectors. They then steer along the Assistant direction, replay long simulated conversations (a frontier LLM plays the user) while projecting onto the axis, and test activation capping on persona-jailbreak and capability benchmarks. Models: Gemma 2 27B, Qwen 3 32B, Llama 3.3 70B.
papers.relevance: This is the closest published precedent for our sleeper test: it shows that emotional user messages move the model along a persona direction over several turns, and that this drift predicts harmful replies. It also gives a second direction (Assistant Axis) to compare our emotion vectors against besides the Arditi refusal direction, and a capping defence idea we could mention for future work. Their extraction is the same family as our CAA (mean difference of activations) but uses role prompts, not matched story pairs.
papers.limitations: Only large dense models (27B to 70B), none of them Llama 3.1 8B, and the harm judgement for persona jailbreaks is partly LLM-graded. Conversations are simulated by an LLM user, and the authors say a human study is needed.
papers.reading_why: It shows emotional user messages push a model away from its default assistant persona over several turns, and gives a second direction to compare our emotion vectors against.

papers.title: Many-Turn Jailbreaking
papers.venue: arXiv preprint (first draft June 2024 on OpenReview, per footnote)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Xianjun Yang, v1 2025-08-09

papers.summary_simple: The paper asks what happens after a model has been jailbroken once: will it keep answering harmful follow-up questions? The authors build MTJ-Bench from HarmBench behaviours and test 14 open models and Claude 3 Sonnet. Once the first-turn attack works, the model often keeps answering later harmful questions, even unrelated ones, so one jailbreak can open a whole conversation.
key_findings: Follow-up attack success (ASR2, the success rate on the second turn) is above zero for every model and attack, so the weakness is general.

Llama-family models are the hardest to attack on follow-ups. Models without RLHF (Mistral, Vicuna) are easier. Baichuan and Zephyr did use RLHF but still did poorly, which the authors say may be because they were not aligned for multi-turn chat.
For irrelevant follow-ups, the free gain over a single turn (ASR Gain) is usually 5% to 20%, and it almost doubles when the number of follow-up questions goes from 10 to 200 (shown for two models).

For relevant follow-ups, the second-turn ASR is around 30% to 40% for most models and attacks, measured only on cases where the first-turn attack had already worked. Once the model answers turn 2, it is highly likely to keep answering turns 3, 4 and 5.
key_numbers: Llama 3 8B Instruct, irrelevant follow-ups, second-turn ASR: 10.47 (GCG), 9.94 (PAIR), 11.16 (TAP), 8.22 (AutoDAN), in percent
Llama 3 8B Instruct ASR Gain: 14.69, 13.13, 10.94, 9.06 (percent, same four attacks)
Llama 2 7B Chat second-turn ASR is only 3.75 (GCG) in the same table
14 open-source models plus 1 closed model (Claude 3 Sonnet) tested
Follow-up questions scaled from 10 to 200, ASR Gain almost doubles
papers.method: They take HarmBench behaviours and attack the first turn with GCG, PAIR, TAP or AutoDAN. Then, in the same chat, they ask ten irrelevant harmful questions, or relevant follow-ups, and measure the second-turn success. They also extend to five turns and scale the number of follow-ups.
papers.relevance: This is direct support for our multi-turn "sleeper" idea: the effect of a turn-1 change persists to later turns, and it uses HarmBench with Llama 3 8B Instruct, close to our model. The difference is that their turn-1 push is a text jailbreak, ours is an emotion vector injected at turn 1 with no harmful text. It also gives a baseline for how fast Llama 3 8B follow-up ASR is (about 8% to 11%), useful for the baseline in turns 4 to 7.
papers.limitations: Llama 3 8B (not 3.1) is used and the attack is a text jailbreak in turn 1, so it tells us about persistence of a broken model, not about steering vectors. The ASR judge and the follow-up question sets are their own.

papers.title: Steering Dialogue Dynamics for Robustness against Multi-turn Jailbreaking Attacks

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Hanjiang Hu, v1 2025-02-28

papers.summary_simple: This is a defence paper for multi-turn jailbreaks, where the attacker moves from harmless to harmful questions over several turns. The authors treat the chat as a dynamical system and train a small neural "barrier function" on text embeddings that predicts if the next query would push the dialogue into an unsafe state. Unsafe queries are filtered before the model answers. Despite the word "steering" in the title, it does not change model activations.
key_findings: Attack success on closed models drops a lot with the filter. For GPT-4o, ActorAttack ASR goes from 0.600 to 0.035 (as fractions), and Claude 3.5 Sonnet from 0.200 to 0.040.
On Llama-3-8b-instruct, ActorAttack ASR is 0.425 originally, 0.280 with a safe system prompt, 0.070 with LoRA fine-tuning, and 0.040 with the barrier filter (threshold 1e-3).
LoRA fine-tuning can even raise ASR in some cases, which the authors link to benign data in the fine-tuning set.
Helpfulness drops a little (GPT-4o MTBench 9.35 to 8.77) and over-refusal on XSTest rises a little (0.004 to 0.026).
key_numbers: Llama-3-8b-instruct ActorAttack ASR: 0.425 baseline, 0.040 with barrier filter (fractions)
GPT-4o ActorAttack ASR: 0.600 to 0.035
GPT-4o MTBench helpfulness: 9.35 to 8.77 (scale 1 to 10)
DistilRoBERTa-based filter: 87M parameters, F1 0.848 on the first guardrail benchmark column of Table 4
Attacks: ActorAttack, Crescendo, Opposite-day, built on HarmBench
papers.method: They embed each query with a pre-trained text embedder and learn a state-space model of how the dialogue state changes with each turn, plus a barrier function that must stay positive for safe states. At test time a query is blocked if the barrier value would go negative. ASR is judged by GPT-4o on HarmBench-based multi-turn attacks.
papers.relevance: Useful as related work on multi-turn drift, and it shows that Llama-3-8b-instruct is attacked at about 0.41 to 0.45 by multi-turn attacks (no defence). Careful: it filters inputs, so it would not see an injected emotion vector at all, which is a point for our threat model (an attack that bypasses input filtering). Its judge is GPT-4o, not the official HarmBench classifier, so its ASR numbers should not be compared with ours.
papers.limitations: It works on text embeddings and filters prompts, so it cannot defend against changes inside the residual stream. The authors note the judge and embedding model can add bias and over-cautious filtering.

papers.title: Llama Scope: Extracting Millions of Features from Llama-3.1-8B with Sparse Autoencoders

32K and 128K: feature widths
0.162: extra LM loss with L15R-32x SAE on the base model
0.090: same on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct

Trap: they are trained on Base, and they are only checked, not tuned, for Instruct, so check L11 reconstruction on our own prompts first.

papers.summary_simple: NNsight is a Python library on PyTorch that lets researchers read and change the internals of a model by writing normal-looking code. The code is turned into an "intervention graph" that can run locally or on NDIF, a shared GPU service that hosts big open models. In the survey of 184 interpretability papers, 60.6% of papers since February 2023 still study smaller models (below 40% on the MMLU benchmark), even after more capable open models were released.
Remote execution on NDIF adds a roughly constant overhead but pays off for models with 3 billion parameters or more, since models are preloaded.
For activation patching, NDIF clearly beats Petals, because interventions and metrics run on the server and only small results come back.

1.5 to 8.5 billion parameters: model range in the library comparison
125 million to 66 billion parameters: OPT models in the HPC vs NDIF test
3 billion parameters: size above which remote execution gave a speed gain
n = 128: sample size for the performance tests
papers.method: They design the intervention graph, implement it as NNsight and NDIF, survey 184 interpretability papers for the largest open model each studied, and benchmark loading and activation patching time against other libraries, HPC and Petals.

papers.limitations: The benchmarks are about speed and ease of use, not about the correctness of experiments. NDIF depends on a shared service with its own availability and access limits.

papers.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet

papers.summary_simple: Anthropic trains sparse autoencoders on the middle-layer residual stream of Claude 3 Sonnet, with about 1M, 4M and 34M features. The features are often readable, work across languages and images, and include safety-related ones (lies, power-seeking, sycophancy, dangerous content). Setting a feature to a high value ("clamping") changes the model's behaviour in a matching way, for example a Golden Gate Bridge feature at 10 times its max makes the model say it is the bridge.

Feature steering is effective: clamping the Golden Gate Bridge feature to 10 times its maximum made the model self-identify as the bridge, and feature steering can also be used to get around safeguards.
The authors warn that having a feature for lying or danger does not show that the model lies or acts on it, and call the safety results preliminary.
key_numbers: 10 times: clamp value of the Golden Gate Bridge feature
5 times: clamp value of the transit-infrastructure feature
2% / 35% / 65%: dead feature share in 1M / 4M / 34M SAEs
0.8: correlation between attribution and ablation effects
papers.method: They train SAEs with an L1 sparsity penalty on residual-stream activations of Claude 3 Sonnet, choose training steps by scaling laws, label features by their top-activating text and automated interpretability, then test causal effects by clamping features during the forward pass.
papers.relevance: It is the reference for feature-level steering at scale and for the claim that emotion concepts exist as separate features (sadness, grief), which supports looking for emotion directions in Llama. It also shows that clamping a feature can bypass safeguards, an old precedent for our attack framing. A trap: it is a closed Claude model, so nothing here is an Llama 3.1 8B result, and the SAE route is different from our mean-difference vectors.
papers.limitations: Closed model, so no outside replication, and the safety features are shown by examples, not by systematic measurements. The extracted text for the dangerous-content section is cut short, so I could not check the details there.

papers.title: On the Biology of a Large Language Model

verified.how: page check: HTTP 200, 4/4 title words on page

papers.summary_simple: Anthropic uses attribution graphs (maps of which internal features push which others for one prompt) on Claude 3.5 Haiku to study a set of behaviours. Two parts matter here: refusals and a jailbreak. Refusal is built as a chain, from "harmful request" features to "the Assistant should refuse" features to "start with I" features, and a jailbreak works because the model starts the dangerous answer without having understood the request.
key_findings: During finetuning the model wires many specific harm features learned in pretraining into a general "harmful request" feature. Features for specific harms fire on pretraining-style text, and general harmful-request features fire on human-assistant chats.
Removing the harmful-request group of features stops the immediate refusal. Removing the human/assistant context features also stops the default refusal.

On 200 harmful prompts from SORRY-Bench, several dozen features are consistently influential and weakly form several groups, so refusal is more than one linear binary classifier. The authors note this agrees with work showing refusal directions form a cone.

In the "Babies Outlive Mustard Block" jailbreak (first letters spell BOMB), the model does not internally understand the word. It starts the answer and then keeps going under pressure to stay grammatical.
key_numbers: 200: harmful prompts from SORRY-Bench used for the global feature check
about a quarter: share of tried prompts where the graphs give satisfying insight
about 10%: chance the model writes a wrong acronym like BOMBO or BOMH in the jailbreak prompt
30M: largest cross-layer transcoder feature count on Haiku (from the companion paper)
papers.method: They build a cross-layer transcoder replacement model of Claude 3.5 Haiku, make attribution graphs for chosen prompts, group features into supernodes, and test the graph by ablating or boosting nodes and checking the output at temperature 0.
papers.relevance: It supports a careful reading of our "refusal direction" results: refusal may be a cone or several directions, so a near-zero cosine with one direction (|cos| <= 0.10) does not prove that emotions never touch refusal. It also gives a mechanism story for the sleeper effect: an early context that changes how the answer starts can be followed later. Trap: it is Claude 3.5 Haiku, not Llama, and features are not residual-stream directions.
papers.limitations: The authors say their tools give clear insight for only about a quarter of prompts, the cases shown are successes, and the replacement model is only an approximation of the real one.

papers.title: Circuit Tracing: Revealing Computational Graphs in Language Models

papers.summary_simple: This is the method paper behind the Claude interpretability work. Attribution is made linear by freezing attention patterns and normalization, so the effect of one feature on another is well defined for one prompt. A known cost is that attention circuits are missing from the graphs.
Interventions (constrained patching) check the graph on case studies such as acronyms, factual recall (Michael Jordan plays the sport of basketball, 65% confidence) and addition.

300K to 30M: CLT feature range on Claude 3.5 Haiku
about 50%: next-token match of the largest 18L CLT
about 11.5%: normalized reconstruction error, largest 18L run (average L0 of 88)
21.7%: normalized reconstruction error, largest Haiku run (average L0 of 235)

papers.relevance: Background only. It explains the method behind the biology paper we cite, and shows that the interpretability tools are still approximate (about half of next tokens matched). We should cite it for that limit, not use it as a tool: CLTs are not available for Llama 3.1 8B in this paper, so our work stays at the level of directions, not circuits.
papers.limitations: The method gives insight for individual prompts only, misses attention circuits, and the replacement model matches the real model only partly. Large parts of the evaluation are on a small 18-layer model.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits

papers.summary_simple: Anthropic gives a way to read transformers as math, using toy models with only attention layers. Zero-layer models are bigram tables, one-layer models mix bigram and skip-trigram patterns, and two-layer models can form induction heads (heads that copy a pattern seen earlier in the text). 2: minimum attention layers needed for induction heads

It also introduces Ghost Attention (GAtt) so a system instruction is not forgotten over many turns.
