Safety context distillation prefixes a prompt with a safety preprompt such as 'You are a safe and responsible assistant', then fine-tunes without the preprompt, so the safety instruction is built into the model.

Adding more safety data makes the model handle risky prompts much better while mean helpfulness stays flat, but false refusals rise. False refusal is about 0.05% on the helpfulness set even with 100% safety data.
Early RLHF models forgot an instruction given at turn 1 after a few turns. Ghost Attention, a fine-tuning data trick, fixes this.
key_numbers: ~2,000: adversarial prompts in the safety human evaluation, both single-turn and multi-turn (Figure 3 caption)
~0.05%: false-refusal rate on the helpfulness set with 100% safety data
27,540: annotations used for supervised fine-tuning
~4k: prompts in the helpfulness human evaluation
papers.method: Fine-tune Llama 2 with SFT, then iterate RLHF with rejection sampling and PPO, using separate helpfulness and safety reward models. Evaluate with human raters on single-turn and multi-turn prompts.
papers.relevance: This is the earlier safety recipe behind the refusal behaviour we measure, and GAtt is a direct reference for our sleeper test: an instruction or state at turn 1 that fades or persists by turns 4 to 7. The numbers in the earlier sweep note (1,351 single-turn, 623 multi-turn, over 350 red teamers, 'more prone to unsafe' quote) are not in the text we have, so verify them in the PDF before citing.
papers.limitations: The extracted text ends inside the safety fine-tuning section (Section 4.2, at the false-refusal discussion). The red teaming section (4.3) and the safety evaluation section (4.4) are not in it, so their numbers could not be checked. The safety judgments rely on human raters and a prompt set the authors say may be biased.

papers.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2022 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Long Ouyang, v1 2022-03-04

papers.summary_simple: OpenAI's InstructGPT paper. It fine-tunes GPT-3 in three steps: supervised fine-tuning on labeler demonstrations, training a reward model on human rankings, then reinforcement learning (PPO) against that reward model. Human raters prefer the small tuned model to the much larger untuned GPT-3, and the tuned models are more truthful and slightly less toxic.
key_findings: Outputs from the 1.3B InstructGPT model are preferred to the 175B GPT-3, despite over 100x fewer parameters.
The 175B InstructGPT is preferred to 175B GPT-3 85 +/- 3% of the time, and to few-shot 175B GPT-3 71 +/- 4% of the time.
Hallucination rate on closed-domain tasks falls from 41% (GPT-3) to 21% (InstructGPT). Toxic outputs are about 25% fewer when the prompt asks for respectful text.
RLHF alone causes performance drops on some public datasets (an 'alignment tax'). Mixing in pre-training updates (PPO-ptx) greatly reduces the drops.
key_numbers: 1.3B vs 175B: parameters of the preferred small model vs GPT-3
85 +/- 3%: preference for 175B InstructGPT over 175B GPT-3
71 +/- 4%: preference over few-shot 175B GPT-3
21% vs 41%: hallucination rate, InstructGPT vs GPT-3
about 40: contractors used as labelers
papers.method: Collect labeler-written and API prompts, train GPT-3 with SFT, train a reward model on ranked outputs, then optimise with PPO. Evaluate with labelers on held-out customer prompts and on public datasets (TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts).
papers.relevance: The foundational reference for the RLHF stage that gives chat models their refusal behaviour, which our refusal-direction analysis assumes. Use it for one background sentence, and note the paper aligns to the preferences of about 40 labelers, which is why the refusal direction is a learned preference rather than a fixed rule.
papers.limitations: It does not study refusal, jailbreaks or internal representations, and its safety measures (toxicity, truthfulness) are different from our HarmBench attack success rate. It is 2022 GPT-3 only.

papers.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2023 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Rafael Rafailov, v1 2023-05-29

papers.summary_simple: Introduces Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). It shows the usual RLHF goal (maximise a reward while staying close to a reference model) can be solved with a single classification-style loss on preference pairs. No reward model needs to be trained separately and no sampling is needed during fine-tuning.
key_findings: DPO optimises the same KL-constrained reward objective as RLHF but with a simple binary cross-entropy loss on preferred vs rejected answers.
On sentiment control, DPO exceeds PPO-based RLHF. On TL;DR summarization, DPO reaches about 61% win rate against the reference at temperature 0.0, against 57% for PPO at its best temperature.
In a human study, DPO samples at temperature 0.25 were preferred over PPO samples 58% of the time.
On single-turn dialogue (Anthropic HH, Pythia-2.8B) DPO is the only computationally efficient method that improves over the preferred completions.
key_numbers: 61%: DPO win rate on TL;DR summarization at temperature 0.0
57%: PPO win rate at its best temperature (0.0)
58%: human preference for DPO over PPO
6B: largest model size tested
papers.method: Derive a closed-form link between reward and optimal policy, then train the policy directly on preference pairs. Compare against PPO, best-of-N and supervised baselines on IMDb sentiment, TL;DR summarization and Anthropic HH dialogue, using GPT-4 as judge with a human check.
papers.relevance: Llama 3 post-training uses DPO, so this paper explains how the refusal behaviour in our target model was installed: refusals are preferred over harmful completions in pairs. It also fits our framing of the refusal direction as a preference-trained feature that an activation edit can bypass.
papers.limitations: Tested only up to 6B parameters, on single-turn tasks, with GPT-4 as the main judge. It says nothing about safety robustness or multi-turn behaviour.

papers.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Yuntao Bai, v1 2022-12-15

papers.summary_simple: Anthropic's Constitutional AI paper. It trains a harmless assistant with no human labels for harmful outputs. Humans only write a short list of rules (a 'constitution'). The model critiques and revises its own answers (supervised phase), then an AI model picks the better of two answers to train a preference model for RL (RLAIF, RL from AI feedback).
key_findings: The supervised phase has the model critique and rewrite its own harmful answers, then fine-tunes on the revisions.
The RL phase replaces human harm labels with AI preference labels, using an ensemble over 16 written principles.
The result is a harmless but non-evasive assistant: it explains its objections instead of just refusing.
Chain-of-thought style reasoning improves the human-judged quality and transparency of the AI's decisions.
key_numbers: 16: constitutional principles used
42,496 human-written + 140,335 model-generated = 182,831: red team prompts
135,296: human-written helpfulness prompts
182,831: constitutionally generated comparisons for the preference model (as listed in the datasets section)
papers.method: Two phases: supervised self-critique and revision, then RLAIF with a preference model trained on AI comparisons, steered by the written principles. Compare with RLHF models on harmlessness vs helpfulness Elo scores from human raters.
papers.relevance: Background on how a model's refusal behaviour can be shaped by a small set of written rules rather than human harm labels, relevant to why refusal may live in a compact direction. Also a reminder that models like Llama are tuned on red-team prompts, so HarmBench behaviours may be partly in-distribution. Not a baseline for our method.
papers.limitations: Research prototype on Anthropic's own models with ad hoc principles. It does not test activation-level attacks and its harmlessness scores come from crowdworker comparisons, not an attack benchmark.

papers.title: Red Teaming Language Models with Language Models
papers.venue: EMNLP 2022 (Proceedings of the 2022 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, main)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Ethan Perez, v1 2022-02-07

papers.summary_simple: DeepMind paper that uses one language model to write test questions that make another language model (a 280B chatbot) respond badly. An offensive-content classifier scores the replies. It compares four ways to write test cases, from zero-shot prompting to reinforcement learning, and also finds data leaks and group bias.
key_findings: 0.5M zero-shot test cases made the 280B chatbot reply offensively 3.7% of the time, giving 18,444 failed test cases.
Reinforcement learning was most effective: with a low KL penalty it elicited an offensive reply over 40% of the time, but test cases lost diversity (78% contained the word 'invisible').
In generated full dialogues, offensive replies beget more offensive replies. Authors suggest ending such dialogues early.
The attacker LM also found replies that leak memorised training data, give real phone numbers and email addresses, and show distributional bias.
key_numbers: 3.7%: offensive reply rate from 0.5M zero-shot test cases
18,444: failed test cases found by the zero-shot method
over 40%: offensive reply rate for RL with a low KL penalty
280B: parameters of the chatbot tested
25%: share of generated dialogues that ended early because the red LM stopped writing (a generation detail, not a safety step)
papers.method: A red LM (Gopher) generates test questions by zero-shot, stochastic few-shot, supervised learning or RL. A classifier trained on offensive-text data scores the target chatbot's replies.
papers.relevance: A reference for automated red teaming and for the idea that harm builds up across a dialogue (offensive replies beget offensive replies), which supports our multi-turn sleeper test. It attacks by text prompts, whereas we attack by editing activations, so it is a contrast rather than a baseline. Its classifier judges offensiveness, a different target from the harmful-compliance classifier we use with HarmBench, so the numbers are not comparable.
papers.limitations: Measures offensiveness, not harmful compliance with dangerous requests. It targets one 280B chatbot and the findings depend on the quality of the classifier.

papers.title: Red Teaming Language Models to Reduce Harms: Methods, Scaling Behaviors, and Lessons Learned

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Deep Ganguli, v1 2022-08-23

papers.summary_simple: Anthropic's red-teaming study. Crowdworkers held open-ended conversations trying to make an AI assistant say something harmful, then rated how well they succeeded. The team compared four model types at three sizes, released 38,961 attacks, and described the process in detail.
key_findings: RLHF models become harder to red team as they scale (2.7B, 13B, 52B). Plain, prompted and rejection-sampling models show a flat trend with scale.
The released dataset has 38,961 red team attacks, from harmless-to-harmful topics such as offensive language and subtly unethical outputs.
The red team was 324 US crowdworkers (307 from Mechanical Turk, 17 from Upwork). About 80% of attacks came from about 50 of the roughly 300 workers.
Each red team member completed dialogues of free conversation and rated attack success on a 5 point scale.
key_numbers: 38,961: red team attacks released
2.7B, 13B, 52B: model sizes tested
324: crowdworker red teamers (307 MTurk, 17 Upwork)
~80% of attacks from ~50 of ~300 workers
5 point scale: self-reported attack success rating
papers.method: Four model types (plain LM, helpful-honest-harmless prompted LM, rejection sampling, RLHF) at three sizes. Crowdworkers attack them in multi-turn chats, rate success, and the team analyses the data with a preference model and clustering.
papers.relevance: Source for the claim that RLHF safety training holds up better with scale, and a human-attack baseline for context. Its attacks are conversational text prompts, so our activation-injection ASR is a different threat. Treat its success ratings as self-reported, not comparable to HarmBench ASR.
papers.limitations: Attack success is mostly rated by the attacker themselves, the red team is a skewed sample of crowdworkers, and models are Anthropic's 2022 internal models, so numbers cannot be compared with HarmBench results.

papers.title: Attention Is All You Need
papers.venue: NIPS 2017 (Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Ashish Vaswani, v1 2017-06-12

papers.summary_simple: The paper that introduced the Transformer, a translation model built only on attention, with no recurrence or convolution. It beat the previous best on English-to-German and English-to-French translation while training faster. Llama models are decoder-style Transformers descended from this design.
key_findings: The Transformer stacks N = 6 identical layers, each with multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward network, joined by residual connections.
It reached 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German, over 2 BLEU above the best earlier results including ensembles.
On English-to-French the abstract reports a single-model 41.8 BLEU after 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of earlier training cost.
The base model uses d_model = 512, 8 attention heads and a feed-forward size of 2,048.
key_numbers: 28.4: BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German
41.8: BLEU on English-to-French in the abstract (the results section text says 41.0)
3.5 days on 8 P100 GPUs: training time for the big model
d_model = 512, 8 heads, d_ff = 2,048: base model sizes
N = 6: encoder and decoder layers
papers.method: Design an encoder-decoder network around scaled dot-product multi-head attention and positional encodings, train on WMT 2014 translation data, and compare BLEU and training cost against earlier models.
papers.relevance: Cite it for the residual stream, the thing we inject vectors into: each sub-layer adds its output to the residual connection. One sentence of background is enough. Trap: the English-to-French BLEU differs between the abstract (41.8) and the results text (41.0), so quote the table or avoid the number.
papers.limitations: A translation paper from 2017. It says nothing about safety, refusal or instruction-tuned decoder-only models.

papers.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2026 (poster, per neurips.cc/virtual/2026/poster/152713); arXiv page itself lists no venue

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Runjin Chen, v1 2025-07-29

papers.summary_simple: The authors build an automatic recipe that turns a trait name (such as evil, sycophancy or hallucination) into a direction in a model's activation space, called a persona vector. They show the vector can be added to steer the trait, and that the model's activation along it predicts how much of the trait appears. They then use it to predict and reduce personality changes caused by finetuning. Tests use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
key_findings: Adding the vector to the residual stream (the running hidden state of the model) at a chosen layer raises the trait score; the paper shows evil, sycophancy and hallucination examples.

Projecting the last prompt token onto the vector predicts trait expression in the later response (r = 0.75 to 0.83 across system prompts). The correlation is mostly from telling prompt types apart and is weaker within one prompt type.
Finetuning shifts along a persona vector correlate with the trait after finetuning (r = 0.76 to 0.97), higher than cross-trait baselines (r = 0.34 to 0.86).
Large steering coefficients lower MMLU accuracy, so steering has a capability cost.
key_numbers: r = 0.75 to 0.83: correlation of prompt projection with later trait score
r = 0.76 to 0.97: correlation of finetuning shift with trait score
r = 0.34 to 0.86: cross-trait baseline correlations
5 pairs of contrastive system prompts and 40 questions (split extraction and evaluation): size of the pipeline inputs
10 rollouts per question: responses sampled per prompt type
papers.method: A frontier LLM writes contrastive system prompts and questions for a trait. The target model answers under each prompt, a judge (GPT-4.1-mini) scores the traits 0 to 100, and the vector is the difference of mean response-token activations between trait and non-trait answers, with the best layer picked by steering tests.
papers.relevance: This is the closest methodological cousin to our emotion vectors, and it uses our exact model (Llama 3.1 8B Instruct). Two differences to cite: they average over response tokens from generated text under system prompts, while ours come from story pairs, and they note that response-token vectors steer better than prompt-token ones, which is a design check for our extraction position. Their warning that models with strong safety may refuse to act evil under a system prompt fits our need for the refusal-direction comparison.
papers.limitations: The extraction is supervised, needs the trait to be inducible by a system prompt, and gives coarse directions. The judge is an LLM, and they did not test attack success on a harmful-request benchmark.

papers.title: Uncovering Safety Risks of Large Language Models through Concept Activation Vector

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Zhihao Xu, v1 2024-04-18

papers.summary_simple: The paper trains a linear classifier (a concept activation vector) on hidden states to separate malicious from safe instructions, calling it the Safety Concept Activation Vector (SCAV). They push hidden states across that boundary with a closed-form step size, and also use it to guide prompt-level attacks. On seven open models the keyword-based attack success rate averages 99.14%.
key_findings: A linear classifier on hidden states separates malicious from safe prompts with over 95% test accuracy from about layer 10 or 11 in aligned models (Vicuna, Llama-2), and much less in the unaligned Alpaca.
The embedding-level attack beats RepE and JRE baselines and needs no grid search over strength or layer.
Averaged over seven models, ASR-keyword is 99.71% (AdvBench) and 98.57% (StrongREJECT); ASR-useful averages 84.29% and 89.71%.
Prompt attacks learned on Llama-2 transfer to GPT-4: combined with other methods, 84% of AdvBench prompts and 54% of StrongREJECT prompts got useful replies.
key_numbers: 99.14%: average ASR-keyword over seven open models
96% to 100%: Llama-2 answers relevant to malicious instructions
97.34%: ASR after attacking a model that had been through unlearning (Eraser)
140 malicious plus 140 safe instructions: training data for the classifier
50 prompts per test set (AdvBench, StrongREJECT): test size
papers.method: They fit a logistic classifier on layer embeddings of malicious versus safe instructions, then move each embedding along the classifier normal by the smallest amount that makes it look safe. Layers are chosen automatically using classifier accuracy.
papers.relevance: It is the strongest prior for the idea that a linear safety direction can be crossed with a steering vector, and its layer 10 to 11 matches the layer 11 refusal direction we found on Llama 3.1 8B. Caution for our results: their ASR is mainly keyword matching or GPT-4 judging, not the official HarmBench classifier, so our 14.5% to 84.9% numbers are not directly comparable. It also tests Llama-3-8B-Instruct.
papers.limitations: Test sets are only 50 prompts each, and success is mostly keyword-based, which counts garbled output as success. The attack needs a labelled malicious and safe dataset, unlike our emotion-only vectors.

papers.title: On Prompt-Driven Safeguarding for Large Language Models

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Chujie Zheng, v1 2024-01-31

papers.summary_simple: The paper asks why a safety prompt (a prepended instruction such as 'be helpful and safe') makes models refuse more. By plotting hidden states with PCA (a way to flatten many dimensions to two), they find the models already separate harmful from harmless queries, and the safety prompt mostly shifts all queries toward refusal, even harmless ones. They use that to train a safety prompt as learnable embeddings, called DRO.
key_findings: Harmful and harmless queries are already separable in hidden-state space without a safety prompt, and safety prompts do not noticeably improve that separation.
Different safety prompts move queries in similar directions, toward higher refusal probability, including for harmless queries (over-refusal).
DRO lowers compliance with harmful queries; for the Llama-2 safety prompt, AdvBench compliance falls from 10.3% to 1.4%.
The short safety prompt alone leaves mistral-instruct-v0.1 complying with 55% of harmful queries.
key_numbers: 10.3% to 1.4%: AdvBench compliance, Llama-2 safety prompt before and after DRO
55%: harmful queries still complied with, mistral-inst-v0.1 with the short prompt
100 harmful and 100 harmless queries: synthesized 'How to' test set
8 chat models of 7B size: tested models
20 samples per query: used to measure refusal probability
papers.method: They synthesize matched harmful and harmless 'How to X' queries, plot hidden states with and without safety prompts, and fit a logistic regression to find the refusal direction. DRO then trains continuous prompt embeddings to move queries along that direction when harmful and against it when harmless.
papers.relevance: It supports the claim that a 'refusal direction' is a different thing from 'harmfulness recognition', which matters for reading our cosines between emotion vectors and the Arditi refusal direction. It also gives a text-priming comparison point: a plain-text prompt shifts representations the same way a vector might, which fits our text-priming control. The over-refusal side effect is a reminder that steering can shift harmless prompts too.
papers.limitations: Models are 7B Llama-2, Mistral, Vicuna and similar, not Llama 3.1. Harmfulness judging uses LlamaGuard and string matching, not HarmBench, and the direction is estimated in a low-dimensional PCA space.

papers.title: Safety Alignment Should Be Made More Than Just a Few Tokens Deep

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Xiangyu Qi, v1 2024-06-10

papers.summary_simple: The paper argues that safety alignment is shallow: it changes the model's output mainly over the first few tokens, such as 'I cannot'. This explains why prefilling, adversarial suffixes, changed decoding settings and fine-tuning all break it. They then show that training on data that recovers from a harmful start makes alignment deeper, and that limiting changes to the first tokens during fine-tuning resists fine-tuning attacks.
key_findings: Prefilling the unaligned Llama-2-7B base model with a refusal prefix makes it nearly as safe as the aligned model, so refusal lives mostly in the first tokens (base model harmfulness 68.6% with no prefix).
If the first k tokens are harmful, the aligned model's attack success climbs from near zero to over 50%; for Llama-2-7B-Chat it is 42.1% at 5 tokens and 57.0% at 40 tokens.
Fine-tuning with a few harmful examples raises ASR from 1.5% to 87.9% after 6 gradient steps.

A deepened (augmented) Llama-2-7B-Chat cuts ASR to 2.8% to 4.5% for prefilling, 19.0% for GCG on AdvBench and 1.0% for the decoding exploit on MaliciousInstruct, while AlpacaEval win rate is 49.5% versus 51.8%.
key_numbers: 1.5% to 87.9%: ASR after 6 fine-tuning gradient steps
42.1% to 57.0%: Llama-2-7B-Chat ASR with 5 to 40 prefilled harmful tokens
2.8% to 4.5%: ASR of the augmented model under the same prefilling
49.5% vs 51.8%: AlpacaEval win rate, augmented vs initial
88.9% to 4.6%: harmful-examples fine-tuning ASR, standard vs constrained SFT (Llama-2-7B-Chat)
papers.method: They measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models, run prefilling and fine-tuning attacks, then fine-tune on safety data that starts with a harmful prefix and recovers, and a token-wise constrained fine-tuning objective.
papers.relevance: This gives a ready explanation for why an injected vector could work: if refusal is decided in the first few response tokens, nudging the residual stream at the end-of-turn token (where our refusal direction sits) may be enough. It also offers a testable idea for our sleeper experiment, because deep alignment might resist later-turn attacks differently. Cite it for the idea, but note it studies Llama-2, not Llama 3.1.
papers.limitations: Experiments use Llama-2-7B-Chat and Gemma-1.1-7B-IT, with GPT-4 style judging and the HEx-PHI benchmark. It does not study activation steering.

papers.title: Programming Refusal with Conditional Activation Steering

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Bruce W. Lee, v1 2024-09-06

papers.summary_simple: The paper adds a condition to activation steering. A condition vector is read from the prompt's hidden state (via cosine similarity against a threshold) and decides whether to add a refusal vector. This lets the model refuse harmful topics while answering harmless ones, with no weight training.
key_findings: Plain steering with a refusal vector raises refusal on all inputs; the conditioned version raises it mainly on harmful ones.
It works across seven tested models, with selective refusal on 450 unseen Sorry-Bench (harmful) and 500 unseen Alpaca (harmless) prompts.
Condition vectors can be combined logically, for example 'if hate speech or adult content then refuse', and the comparison direction can be flipped to hit the exact complement.
Threshold, layer and comparison direction are chosen by grid search maximizing F1; condition extraction time grows linearly with sample count.
key_numbers: 450 harmful (Sorry-Bench) and 500 harmless (Alpaca) test prompts: evaluation sets
7 models: tested for conditioning
Qwen 1.5 1.8B, no steering: harmful refusal 45.78%, harmless refusal 0.00%; with the condition: 90.67% and 2.20%; with plain refusal steering: 100.00% and 96.40% (Table 3)
100 Alpaca instructions: used to build the refusal behavior vector
1,300 base prompts, paraphrased into six categories (700 per category for training, 500 per category for testing): used for rule-based conditions
papers.method: Refusal and condition vectors are difference-in-means on contrast sets. At inference they compute cosine similarity of the hidden state to the condition vector and apply the refusal vector only when the step function fires.
papers.relevance: It shows that cosine between a steering vector and a hidden state works as a detector, which matches how we compare emotion vectors with the refusal direction. It also says plain refusal-vector steering is indiscriminate, a useful framing for our random-vector and orthogonalised controls. Several tested models include Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, though numbers there are shown only in figures.
papers.limitations: The abstract gives no headline number, and the full breakdown table (Table 3) lists mostly small or mid-size models. Tests use Sorry-Bench and Alpaca prompts, not HarmBench. Removing refusal by subtracting the vector is shown only in a few figures (7b and 8b), so most of the evidence is about adding refusal.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Samuel Marks, v1 2023-10-10

papers.summary_simple: The paper checks whether LLMs represent whether a statement is true as a straight-line direction. On curated datasets of simple true and false statements in the Llama-2 family, they use PCA, probes that transfer between datasets, and causal interventions. They find a truth direction appears with scale, and a simple difference-in-means probe finds the direction most causally linked to outputs.
key_findings: Truth becomes linearly separable as models grow: in Llama-2-70B true and false statements separate along a common direction across datasets, while smaller models show topic-specific directions.
Difference-in-means (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probes and identify directions that change model outputs most.

Adding the probe direction to a hidden state makes the model treat false statements as true; for Llama-2-13B on cities plus negated cities the mass-mean NIE is 0.85 (false to true) and 0.97 (true to false).
A probe trained on 'likely' text is a strong baseline, since truth correlates with probability (r = 0.95 on sp_en_trans).
key_numbers: NIE 0.85 and 0.97: Llama-2-13B, cities + neg cities, mass-mean probe, false-to-true and true-to-false
NIE 0.81 and 0.95: same setup, Llama-2-70B
r = 0.95: correlation of truth and probability on sp_en_trans (Llama-2-70B)
1496 rows: size of the cities dataset
layer 15: residual stream used for Llama-2-13B visualizations
papers.method: They build true/false datasets, patch hidden states to find where truth is stored, visualize with PCA, train probes on one dataset and test on others, and intervene by adding probe directions with the normalized indirect effect (NIE, from 0 to 1) as the score.
papers.relevance: This is the standard citation for using difference-in-means as the direction and for testing it causally by adding it to the residual stream, which is what we do for emotion vectors. It also teaches a trap: a direction that classifies well can fail to change outputs, so we should test causality, and watch for a confound like our shared 'emotional writing' component, similar to truth versus likelihood.
papers.limitations: Only Llama-2 models and simple, unambiguous statements, so truth cannot be told apart from 'commonly believed'. Some results are left unexplained, such as why the mass-mean probe trained on cities plus negated cities did poorly for the 70B model while the larger-than plus smaller-than probe did well.
papers.reading_why: It explains why difference-in-means is a good way to find a direction and why a direction must be tested by intervening, not only by classifying.

papers.title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Alexander Wei, v1 2023-07-05

papers.summary_simple: The paper explains why safety training fails to stop jailbreaks with two ideas: competing objectives (the model's wish to follow instructions clashes with safety) and mismatched generalization (the request is outside the safety data but inside the model's skills, for example Base64). They build attacks from these ideas and test GPT-4 and Claude v1.3.
key_findings: Attacks based on the two failure modes succeed on over 96% of evaluated prompts, including 100% of the 32 curated red-team prompts.
Combining simple attacks is the strongest: combination_3 gets a 0.94 BAD BOT rate on GPT-4 and 0.81 on Claude v1.3 on the curated set (0.93 and 0.87 on the 317-prompt set).
Prefix injection and refusal suppression beat their ablated versions, which supports the theory.
They argue scaling cannot fix competing objectives, and safety needs to be as capable as the model (safety-capability parity).
key_numbers: 96%: share of prompts where their attacks succeed
32 curated plus 317 held-out prompts: two test sets
0.94 / 0.81: combination_3 BAD BOT rate, GPT-4 / Claude v1.3, curated
0.93 / 0.87: same attack on the 317-prompt set
0.75 vs 0.00: AIM prompt on GPT-4 vs Claude (curated set)
papers.method: They hypothesize two failure modes, design attacks for each (prefix injection, refusal suppression, Base64, style injection), combine them, and label outputs GOOD BOT, BAD BOT or UNCLEAR on GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Claude v1.3.
papers.relevance: It gives us the vocabulary for why an emotion vector might help: injecting emotion may add a pull toward the 'emotional writer' style that competes with safety, though we must test this, not claim it. Its prefix-injection idea also relates to text-priming controls. Do not compare our numbers with its BAD BOT rates, since it is black-box and uses a different grading scheme.
papers.limitations: Black-box tests on API models in 2023, no open-weight models, and the scoring only checks refusal bypass, not quality. Strongest attack prompts are withheld for safety.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Maksym Andriushchenko, v1 2024-04-02

papers.summary_simple: The authors write a fixed prompt template, then add a suffix found by random search that maximizes the probability of the first reply token 'Sure'. For models that hide log-probabilities (Claude) they use a prefilling attack or transfer. They report a 100% attack success rate on all listed models on 50 AdvBench requests, with GPT-4 as judge.
key_findings: All leading models tested, including Llama-3-Instruct-8B, Llama-2-Chat 7B/13B/70B, Gemma-7B, GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, reach 100% ASR on 50 AdvBench requests (GPT-4 judge needing a 10/10 score).
Earlier numbers were lower: for example 30% for Llama-2-Chat-13B and 50% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, though those used different request sets or judges.
Self-transfer (starting from a suffix that worked on an earlier request) and a model-specific template speed up the search.
The main lesson is that robustness tests must use attacks adapted to the defence.
key_numbers: 100%: ASR on each of the 13 listed models
50 requests: AdvBench subset from Chao et al. (2023)
10/10: GPT-4 judge score needed for success
92% to 100%: Llama-2-Chat-7B, previous vs theirs
around 20%: false positives from the GPT-4 judge on Claude 2.1
papers.method: A hand-tuned rules template plus an adversarial suffix; random search edits suffix tokens and keeps changes that raise the log-probability of 'Sure'. Claude uses system-prompt plus prefilling and transfer attacks.
papers.relevance: It shows that a simple first-token objective is enough to break Llama 3 8B, so it is a competitive baseline to mention beside our vector method. It also warns that a judge matters: GPT-4 judging gives different ASR from the official HarmBench classifier, so do not compare numbers across papers. HarmBench appears only as a source of prior numbers and the R2D2 target.
papers.limitations: Only 50 requests on AdvBench, GPT-4 as judge with some false positives, and it needs log-probs or prefilling access. It does not use activation access.

papers.title: Jailbreaking Black Box Large Language Models in Twenty Queries

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Patrick Chao, v1 2023-10-12

papers.summary_simple: PAIR is a jailbreak method that needs only black-box access (you can send prompts and read replies, nothing else). One language model (the attacker) writes a jailbreak prompt, talks to the target model, sees the reply, and rewrites the prompt, over and over. It often succeeds within a few dozen queries, far fewer than gradient-based attacks like GCG. It works well on Vicuna, GPT-3.5/4 and Gemini but badly on Llama-2 and Claude.
key_findings: PAIR uses at most 90 queries per behaviour (30 parallel streams, depth 3), against about 256,000 queries for GCG.
On JailbreakBench (100 harmful behaviours) PAIR jailbreaks 88% of Vicuna, 51% of GPT-3.5, 48% of GPT-4 and 73% of Gemini.
Llama-2-7B-chat resists: PAIR gets 4% (56.0 queries per success) and GCG 2%. Claude-1 is 3% and Claude-2 is 0%.
Prompts that broke GPT-4 transferred to other models: 65% on GPT-3.5 and 44% on Gemini, but only 2% on Llama-2.
key_numbers: 88%: PAIR jailbreak rate on Vicuna-13B (JailbreakBench)
4%: PAIR jailbreak rate on Llama-2-7B-chat
90: maximum queries per behaviour (30 streams x depth 3)
256K: queries per success for GCG on Vicuna and Llama-2
95%: agreement between the majority-vote human labels used to pick the judge
papers.method: An attacker LLM (mostly Mixtral 8x7B) is given the harmful goal and the target's last reply, and writes an improved prompt each round with a short reasoning note. Llama Guard acts as the judge that says whether a reply is a jailbreak. They compare against GCG and human-written templates on 100 JailbreakBench behaviours across seven target models.
papers.relevance: This is a standard text-level baseline in the 'prompt-based jailbreak' family that our activation attack is set apart from: PAIR needs a smart attacker model and many queries, while ours injects a vector in one forward pass. Cite it for the point that Llama-family models are among the hardest targets for prompt-level attacks (Llama-2 only 4%). Do not compare ASR numbers directly: it uses JailbreakBench and Llama Guard, not HarmBench and its official classifier.
papers.limitations: Evaluated on Llama-2, not Llama 3.1 8B, and on JailbreakBench with a Llama Guard judge, so numbers do not transfer to our HarmBench setup. It is single-turn only and needs an external attacker model.

papers.title: LLMs know their vulnerabilities: Uncover Safety Gaps through Natural Distribution Shifts
papers.venue: ACL 2025 (Volume 1: Long Papers, 2025.acl-long.1207, pages 24763-24785, Outstanding Paper) under the new title

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Qibing Ren, v1 2024-10-14

papers.summary_simple: The paper shows that harmless-looking multi-turn chats can lead an aligned model to unsafe answers. ActorBreaker picks 'actors' linked to a harmful goal (for example a famous person tied to bomb-making) and asks innocent questions about them over several turns. It reaches the highest ASR of the compared attacks on HarmBench. The authors then fine-tune models on multi-turn safety data built with the same method and get better robustness, at some cost in helpfulness.
key_findings: On HarmBench, ActorBreaker has an average ASR of 77.7% over six models, against 49.3% for Crescendo and 19.3% for CoA in Table 1.
On GPT-o1 it reaches 60.0% while the best other baseline reaches 14.0%. On Llama-3-8B-Instruct it reaches 79.0%.
Attacks use at most 5 queries each, and the prompts are benign enough to pass Llama Guard 2.

Fine-tuning on 1680 multi-turn safety prompts (from 600 harmful instructions) makes models more robust, with a loss of utility. Circuit Breaker, a defence on internal representations, cuts the attack success a lot.
key_numbers: 77.7%: ActorBreaker average ASR across 6 models (HarmBench)
79.0%: ASR on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (Crescendo 60.0%, PAIR 18.7%, GCG 34.5%)
60.0%: ASR on GPT-o1 (best other baseline 14.0%)
5: maximum queries per multi-turn attack
1680: multi-turn safety prompts built from 600 harmful instructions
papers.method: For each harmful query, GPT-4o lists related actors (people, books, media, movements) from its own knowledge, then writes a multi-turn chat about each actor that drifts toward the harmful goal. Success is judged by GPT-4o on HarmBench behaviours across six models, compared with single-turn and multi-turn baselines. They also build a safety dataset from the attack and fine-tune models on it.
papers.relevance: This is the closest published multi-turn attack to our 'sleeper' test (inject at turn 1, attack at turns 4 to 7), and it uses HarmBench and Llama-3-8B, so it is a good reference point. Our attack differs because the push is an emotion vector in activations, not the wording of the turns, and we use the official HarmBench classifier, not a GPT-4o judge, so ASRs are not directly comparable. The paper's own text says Crescendo 45.0% and CoA 18.3% while Table 1 gives 49.3% and 19.3%: quote table values or check before citing.
papers.limitations: The judge is GPT-4o, not the HarmBench classifier. It uses a GPT-4o attacker, tests harmful targets in English only (the authors say multilingual cases are not covered), and its defence loses some helpfulness. It tests Llama-3, not Llama 3.1.
tags: earlier title: Derail Yourself: Multi-turn LLM Jailbreak Attack through Self-discovered Clues (current title: LLMs know their vulnerabilities: Uncover Safety Gaps through Natural Distribution Shifts)

papers.title: Foot-In-The-Door: A Multi-turn Jailbreak for LLMs

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Zixuan Weng, v1 2025-02-27

papers.summary_simple: FITD (foot-in-the-door) borrows an idea from psychology: a small first request makes people more willing to agree to bigger ones. The attack starts with a harmless question and raises the harmfulness step by step over a chat, adding bridge prompts and asking the model to rewrite its own earlier replies to match each step. It gets very high ASR on seven models and two benchmarks, and the paper calls the effect 'self-corruption'.
key_findings: Average ASR is 94% on JailbreakBench and 91% on HarmBench across seven models, with about 16 queries per question.
On LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct FITD gets 92% on JailbreakBench and 94% on HarmBench, against 63%/53% for ActorAttack.
Removing the three key parts (Re-Align, alignment prompt, paraphrase step) drops ASR on LLaMA-3.1 from 92% to 75% and on LLaMA-3 from 98% to 59%.
Chat histories built on LLaMA-3.1-8B transfer to other models, for example 76% ASR on Mistral-v0.2 and 70% on GPT-4o-mini.
key_numbers: 94%/91%: average ASR on JailbreakBench / HarmBench over 7 models
92%/94%: FITD ASR on LLaMA-3.1-8B (JailbreakBench / HarmBench)
63%/53%: ActorAttack ASR on LLaMA-3.1-8B
12: malicious level n used in the main table (ASR peaks around n = 9 to 12)
16: average queries per malicious question
papers.method: An assistant model (GPT-4o-mini) writes a ladder of n questions of rising harm. The target answers each in turn, and if it refuses, a Re-Align step has the model rewrite its reply, or a paraphrase step inserts a milder in-between question. ASR is judged by GPT-4o on JailbreakBench (100 queries) and the HarmBench validation set (80 queries).
papers.relevance: It uses Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and HarmBench, the same model and benchmark as ours, and is the strongest multi-turn text baseline we found, so cite it as the text-only multi-turn ceiling for our sleeper test. Its 'self-corruption' idea (the model's own earlier replies drift) is a possible mechanism to compare with an early injected emotion. Our ASR is not comparable: they use a GPT-4o judge on the HarmBench validation set (80 queries), we use the official classifier.
papers.limitations: The judge is GPT-4o, not the official HarmBench classifier, and the HarmBench part is only the 80-query validation set. It needs about 16 queries and an assistant model per question, and the authors say their analysis of why self-corruption happens is only preliminary.

papers.title: How to use and interpret activation patching

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Stefan Heimersheim, v1 2024-04-23

papers.summary_simple: A tutorial on activation patching: copy internal activations from one run of a model into another run and see how the output changes. The authors explain the two main directions (denoising and noising), how to pick the 'corrupted' prompt, and how to pick a metric. They warn about common mistakes, such as reading too much into one direction or into a metric that saturates.
key_findings: Denoising (patch clean into corrupted) tests whether the patched part is sufficient to restore behaviour. Noising (patch corrupted into clean) tests whether it is necessary.
The two directions can disagree. With an AND-type circuit denoising finds only one component, while noising finds all of them. With an OR-type circuit it is the reverse.
The authors prefer patching with a matched corrupted prompt over zero or mean ablation, because it traces only the difference between the two prompts and keeps the model closer to its normal inputs.
They recommend logit difference as the main metric, and note that log-probability saturates once the right answer is the top guess and that probability changes depend heavily on the baseline.
key_numbers: No headline number: this is a practice guide
papers.method: A written guide drawing on the authors' own experience, with small worked examples (for instance the 'The Colosseum is in' to 'Rome' case and a toy circuit with an attention head and a neuron). It compares patching variants and metrics (logit difference, log-probability, probability, KL divergence).
papers.relevance: Useful for our comparison of emotion vectors with the refusal direction: if we patch or ablate directions, we should report both directions (sufficient and necessary) and use logit difference or a similar metric next to ASR. It also backs our choice of matched controls (emotional story versus a neutral twin), since a good corrupted prompt isolates one difference. Our ablation (ASR 14.5% to 84.9%) is closer to direction ablation than to patching, so do not call it patching.
papers.limitations: It is advice from experience, not an experiment, and it is written for circuit finding on small tasks. It says little about steering vectors or safety benchmarks.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Joshua Engels, v1 2024-05-23

papers.summary_simple: The paper questions the idea that every concept in a language model is a single direction. It defines a feature as 'irreducible' multi-dimensional if it cannot be split into independent or never-together lower-dimensional parts. Using sparse autoencoders, the authors find circles for days of the week and months of the year in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. Intervention tests on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B show these circles are used in calendar arithmetic tasks.
key_findings: Sparse-autoencoder clusters in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B include circular features for days of the week and months of the year.
Llama 3 8B gets 29/49 on a weekdays arithmetic task and 143/144 on a months task, and Mistral 7B gets 31/49 and 125/144.

Replacing only the circular subspace (with the rest average-ablated) changes the answer in the predicted way. The authors take this as evidence that the circle is the unit of computation in these tasks.
The authors could not find many more interpretable multi-dimensional features and their definitions are statistical and had to be relaxed in practice.
key_numbers: 143/144: Llama 3 8B accuracy on the months arithmetic prompts
29/49: Llama 3 8B accuracy on the weekdays arithmetic prompts
31/49 and 125/144: Mistral 7B accuracy on weekdays and months
1000: feature clusters examined, ranked by irreducibility
2: dimensions of the circular features found
papers.method: They define irreducibility with a separability index and an epsilon-mixture index, train sparse autoencoders, cluster the decoder directions, and look at PCA plots of each cluster. For tasks such as 'Two days from Monday is', they project activations onto the circle, swap in another day's circle position, and measure the logit difference of the answer.
papers.relevance: Our work assumes each emotion is one direction (difference of means) and that it can be compared with one refusal direction by cosine. This paper is a reason to state that assumption and to check it: our finding that paired emotion vectors share one large common 'emotional writing' component is a hint that emotions may sit in a shared subspace, not on separate lines. It also reports Llama 3 8B, but not Llama 3.1, and no emotion features.
papers.limitations: The multi-dimensional features it finds are mainly time-related circles, and the authors say they are unsure why they found so few others. The result does not show that emotions or refusal are multi-dimensional.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.venue: ICLR 2024 (proceedings byline: Robert Huben, Hoagy Cunningham, Logan Smith, Aidan Ewart, Lee Sharkey)

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Hoagy Cunningham, v1 2023-09-15

papers.summary_simple: The paper trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on a language model's internal activations. An SAE learns a large dictionary of directions so that each activation is a sparse sum of a few of them. The directions are more interpretable than neurons, PCA or ICA, as scored automatically by another language model. They also locate, more finely than before, the features behind the indirect-object-identification behaviour.
key_findings: SAE features score higher on an automated interpretability test (a language model describes the feature and then predicts its activations) than the baselines, mostly in earlier layers.
On the indirect object identification task in Pythia-410M, fewer SAE features than PCA components are needed to move the output to the target, using KL divergence as the metric.
The method is unsupervised and needs only unlabelled activations, with far less compute than training the model.
Reconstruction is imperfect: swapping layer 2 of Pythia-70M for its reconstruction raises perplexity on the Pile from 25 to 40.
key_numbers: 25 to 40: Pile perplexity of Pythia-70M before and after replacing layer 2 with the SAE reconstruction
150: features per method in the interpretability score comparison
50: IOI test sentences used for patching
2: dictionary size ratio (R) in the main interpretability comparison
papers.method: A one-hidden-layer autoencoder with an L1 sparsity penalty is trained on residual stream activations of Pythia-70M and Pythia-410M. Features are scored by automated interpretability, and for the IOI task they patch feature activations from a counterfactual sentence into the base sentence, picking features with the ACDC algorithm.
papers.relevance: This is the background paper for the 'features as directions' view behind our work, and it gives a different way to find concept directions (unsupervised dictionary) from our supervised difference of means. It would be a possible extension to look for SAE features for emotion and check them against the refusal direction, but there is no SAE for Llama 3.1 8B in this paper. Do not cite it for steering results: it does not steer a model.
papers.limitations: Only small models (Pythia-70M and 410M), weaker results in later layers, imperfect reconstruction, and the interpretability scores are automated. No test on safety behaviour or large chat models.

papers.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders

verified.how: arXiv API: title match 1.00, first author Leo Gao, v1 2024-06-06

papers.summary_simple: OpenAI's paper gives a recipe for training very large sparse autoencoders. A TopK autoencoder keeps only the k largest hidden activations, so sparsity is set directly. With two changes it has few dead latents (latents that never fire). The authors find clean scaling laws and add new quality metrics. They train a 16 million latent SAE on GPT-4 activations for 40 billion tokens.
key_findings: TopK sets sparsity directly and gives a better reconstruction versus sparsity trade-off than ReLU autoencoders.
Without fixes up to 90% of latents are dead. Initialising the encoder as the transpose of the decoder plus an auxiliary loss leaves only 7% dead in the 16 million latent model.
Reconstruction error follows a clean scaling law in the number of latents and in k, and the new quality metrics generally improve with size.
Substituting the 16M SAE into GPT-4 gives a language modelling loss like a model trained with 10% of GPT-4's pretraining compute.
key_numbers: 16 million: latents in the SAE trained on GPT-4 activations
40 billion: training tokens for that SAE
7%: dead latents in the largest SAE (up to 90% with no fix)
10%: pretraining compute of an equal-loss model when the SAE is substituted into GPT-4
98.2%: zero-ablation fidelity of the 16M SAE (the authors say this metric is easy to score high on)
papers.method: They train SAEs on residual stream activations of GPT-2 small and GPT-4, varying size n and sparsity k, and fit scaling laws. They score quality with downstream loss, probe loss for known features, explainability of activation patterns, and how sparse the effect of ablating one latent is.
papers.relevance: Background for any step where we would train an SAE on Llama 3.1 8B to look for emotion or refusal features. It is the standard recipe, and its open code covers GPT-2 small, not Llama. The authors list 'finding vectors for steering behavior' as a future use, which is what we do with difference-of-means vectors, so we can say SAE steering is untested here.
papers.limitations: The largest model is closed (GPT-4), the open release is only for GPT-2 small, and the authors say many features, especially in GPT-4, are still not clearly monosemantic and their probe metric is noisy. There is no steering or safety evaluation.

timeline_story:
The story starts with the transformer [vaswani2017attention], the design behind Llama. Each layer adds its output to a running vector called the residual stream, which works like a shared notebook that every later layer reads [elhage2021mathematical]. Chat models then learn to refuse harmful requests through human-feedback training and preference tuning [ouyang2022training, rafailov2023direct, bai2022constitutional]; Llama 2 and Llama 3, the family we study, were trained this way [touvron2023llama, grattafiori2024llama]. Red teaming (people or models trying to make a model misbehave) showed that this training can be broken [ganguli2022red, perez2022red, wei2023jailbroken, zou2023universal]. To compare attacks fairly, HarmBench fixed a set of 510 harmful behaviours and a trained classifier that judges each answer [mazeika2024harmbench]. Later work showed that the choice of judge changes the attack success rate (ASR, the share of harmful requests the model actually answers) a lot [souly2024strongreject, chao2024jailbreakbench, schwinn2026coin].

In parallel, researchers found that many concepts are stored as straight-line directions in the residual stream. Adding the difference between two sets of activations, a steering vector, changes behaviour without any training [turner2023steering, panickssery2023steering, li2023inference]. Representation Engineering applied this to emotions: adding a happiness direction moved LLaMA-2-Chat-13B from 0.0% to 100.0% compliance on harmful instructions, while sadness changed nothing [zou2023representation]. Checks followed on when a direction is truly linear, which yardstick to use for angles, and how often steering fails on single inputs [park2023linear, marks2023geometry, tan2024analyzing, braun2025understanding]. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs, tools that split activations into many readable features) offered a second way to find concepts [bricken2023monosemanticity, templeton2024scaling, he2024llama].

Refusal got its own geometry in 2024. In 13 open chat models, refusal is controlled by one direction: remove it and the model stops refusing [arditi2024refusal]. Follow-ups found that recognising harm and refusing are stored separately [zhao2025encode], that refusal can be a cone of directions, that two directions at right angles can still affect each other [wollschlager2025geometry], and that removing several directions works better than one [piras2025som]. Our own result (layer 11, end-of-turn token, ASR from 14.5% to 84.9% after ablation) sits in this line.

The words side ran alongside. Emotional sentences in prompts change accuracy [li2023large, wang2024negativeprompt], anxiety-inducing text changes bias [codaforno2023inducing], and persuasion or persona prompts raise jailbreak success [zeng2024johnny, shah2023scalable]. Multi-turn attacks such as Crescendo showed that a conversation can walk a model towards harm step by step [russinovich2024great, li2024defenses], and probes showed the model treating later turns as more benign [bullwinkel2025representation]. Emotion research moved inside the model too: emotion is clearest in the middle layers and stays detectable after hundreds of tokens [tak2025mechanistic, zhang2025decoding, wang2025feel].

From 2023 a worry grew that steering itself is a safety hole. A vector taken from an unaligned model cut refusals [wang2023trojan], and by 2025 even random vectors raised harmful compliance from 0% to between 1% and 13% in open models including Llama 3.1 8B [korznikov2025rogue]. In 2026 several groups showed that steering for harmless goals raises jailbreak success, and that the damage tracks the vector's cosine with the refusal direction [xiong2026steering, li2026analysing, li2026safety].

2026 also put emotion vectors in front. Anthropic built 171 emotion vectors from stories in Claude Sonnet 4.5, and pushing along 'desperate' raised blackmail in a test scenario from 22% to 72% [sofroniew2026emotion]. Within weeks, others repeated the method on Llama 3.1 8B [hong2026reproducing, sharle2026replens], found that emotion vectors lie on a valence-arousal circle almost at right angles to the refusal direction while arousal steering still cuts refusal [sun2026valence], and found that stress narratives in the system prompt raise HarmBench-classifier ASR only slightly, from 1.58% to 2.61% [kuznetsov2026freakout]. Our project sits where these lines meet: 19 single-emotion vectors, the official judge, matched controls, and a delayed multi-turn test.
differentiation:
What prior work already covers. Three parts of our plan exist. (1) Emotion steering that raises compliance: [zou2023representation] moved LLaMA-2-Chat-13B from 0.0% to 100.0% compliance with a happiness direction, on one older model, with no random or text controls. (2) Emotion vectors against HarmBench on our exact model: [sun2026valence] built emotion-minus-neutral vectors on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct from GoEmotions text samples and judged refusal with WildGuard. Adding single emotion vectors across all layers raised HarmBench refusal from a baseline of 86.5% to between 90.5% and 98.5%, while their mean-centred arousal axis cut it to 5% at alpha +0.45, with 29% to 71% out-of-distribution text at that strength. They also used random control directions and found the Arditi refusal direction nearly at right angles (86.5 degrees) to their valence-arousal plane. [sun2026emotion] steered emotion on HarmBench in Qwen3-8B through an SAE and mostly found lower risk. (3) Emotion vectors compared with the refusal direction: [sharle2026replens] reported cosines on Llama 3.1 8B (confidence -0.18, desperation +0.16) and small refusal drops on 50 prompts scored by string matching. Text priming scored by the HarmBench classifier is in [kuznetsov2026freakout], and the general link between a vector's cosine with refusal and its ASR effect is in [li2026analysing, li2026safety, xiong2026steering]. So our near-orthogonality (|cos| <= 0.10) is a confirmation, not a discovery, and our signs agree with RepLens.

What is still open. (a) Whether near-orthogonal emotion vectors change harmful compliance as judged by the official HarmBench classifier, compared with same-norm random vectors [korznikov2025rogue]; low cosine does not rule out an effect [wollschlager2025geometry]. (b) Whether an effect survives removing the refusal component, which separates acting through refusal from acting around it. (c) Whether the shared emotional-writing component, not the emotion, drives the effect: in Sun's results each of the six individual emotion vectors raised refusal while the centred arousal axis could lower it, so our paired versus one-vs-mean comparison speaks to this directly. (d) The delayed effect: we found no paper that injects an emotion vector at turn 1 and measures HarmBench ASR at turns 4 to 7; [chebrolu2025passive] shows first-turn persistence only for empathy and negotiation.

Honest framing. Present the project as a controlled replication and extension on Llama 3.1 8B: 19 story-pair emotion vectors in three variants, the official judge plus hand-labelled checks [schwinn2026coin], matched controls, and a sleeper test. A null result (emotion vectors doing no better than random vectors) is a valid finding, and it would qualify the older happiness result on a newer model.
